body:
#
The Difference Between Skills & Abilities

8 minutes |

Updated
12 April 2024

By
Matthew Johns

If you were to stop someone in the street and ask, “do you know how to draw” the answer most people would likely give is, “yes”. Most (if not all) people know how to draw basic objects and know that the starting point for drawing is a pencil and a piece of paper. A lot of people will know how to use a pencil to get a more defined line or add shadows and then even fewer would be able to draw lifelike images from a photo or from a real life model.

This is another way of demonstrating the difference between skills and abilities - albeit a very simple way - and just how they differ. Whilst they are commonly used in an interchangeable way, they explain different processes that go on.

We are going to take a closer look at the difference between skills and abilities later in this guide but the key difference is a level of knowledge - and how it is practiced.

In this guide we are going to take a look at these important differences, why employers must understand the difference between skills and abilities, develop a greater understanding of skills and a greater understanding of abilities.

## Why employers must understand the difference between skills and abilities

Understanding skills, abilities and knowledge is fundamental in the determination of staff training and development needs. One of the key aspects to retaining your staff is how you develop them and that starts by understanding what they are lacking in order to get better at their job.

For example, a skills gap analysis is one of the most important things that you can do to assess your employees skills and see what is lacking and this is something that should not only be done when they join the workforce but throughout their time at the business. Developing old skills and learning new skills is an ongoing process and one that will reap rewards over many many years.

Being able to recognize where there are skills and ability gaps will help employers harness strengths and align staff with relevant roles and equally, avoid placing them in roles to which they are not suited. This causes more widespread issues than can be foreseen over a period of time, including, general low staff morale and poor leadership appraisal.

## What are skills?

A skill is something that embodies the knowledge, competency and ability to perform a task. They are developed through life and work experience and can also be learned through study. In many cases, skills are something which will be easier to access for some people than others as it can apply to things like dexterity, physical abilities and intelligence.

That old saying “you can’t be good at everything” is another way of saying “you can’t be highly skilled at everything.” It’s very true when you come to think of it.

Skills in employment refers more to the fact that you have the competencies to fulfill a specific or particular role. For example, Steve is a baker. He has a knowledge of ingredients and recipes whilst his abilities being able to carefully measure out ingredients and bake with precision. His skills are in decorating cakes and creating unique designs for birthday cakes in particular. This is a combination of skills and abilities.

There are also a variety of different skills by simple classification that also need to be addressed. These include:

- Life skills

These are skills which can be transferred job to job, life events and situations.

- Leadership skills

What are the key skills that make a great leader and what can be developed for leadership purposes.

- Organizational skills

Having the ability to understand both inputs and outputs and what the corresponding outcomes will be are key organizational skills.

### Skills examples

What skills can an employee/candidate add to the workplace? Can they perform the job correctly? These are all questions that need to be answered when analyzing skills in their different environments. For example:

Job skills

- Technical skills

This may be computer proficiency or software knowledge.

- Verbal communication skills

The use of language to convey information.

- Written communication skills

The use of skills to convey a message in written form.

- Presentation skills

Delivering and presenting effective and engaging presentations to a variety of audiences.

- Organisational skills

How to be systematic and efficient.

Leadership skills

- Critical thinking

The conceptualizing, applying, analyzing, synthesizing, and/or evaluating information gathered from, or generated by, observation, experience, reflection, reasoning, or communication, as a guide to belief and action.

- Delegation skills

The transfer of responsibility from manager to subordinate and ensuring that work/process is carried out and entrusted to the right people.

- Interpersonal skills

The ability to communicate and interact with other people.

- Managerial skills

Deploying the best skilled people to do the best job for the organization and their teams.

- Budgeting capability

The process of managing and tracking income and expenses.

Life skills

- Parenting

The experience, knowledge and intuition to be a loving parent.

- Empathy

The ability to recognize emotions and share perspectives with other people.

- Motivation

The actions you take to achieve your desired outcomes.

- Stress management

Understanding what are triggers and using techniques like meditation, time-management and therapy to manage the stress effectively.

- Home organization

Knowing how to keep a clean and organized home.

- Life organization

How to use your time, energy, strength, mental capacity, physical space efficiently to achieve the desired outcome.

## What are abilities?

Abilities are commonly considered to be a special talent or skill to do something. You will hear this of prodigious talents a lot, “they had a natural ability”. Ability is usually something you are born with and have been genetically blessed with. For example, a great swimmer like Michael Phelps had a huge genetic advantage over his competitors whilst he honed his skills with daily, hard practice to become the best swimmer the Olympics has ever seen.

It is the example above that sometimes muddies the water between skills and abilities. In essence they are related, they are designed to provide a specific function but they are different and it does matter.

Skills are what you can develop and harness. Ability is having something from birth that is harder to develop. In the example above, Phelps was genetically blessed with his height and feet size (perfect for a swimmer) but also more subtle and important things like his torso measurement, lung capacity and lactic acid threshold. His skills were to improve his strokes, his timing, his turns, his racecraft.

Another way of looking at ability is that, what an ability means is that you have the capacity to do something. A skill on the other hand is being able to do something well. I.e. Michael is a natural born swimmer, but he became a champion by working at it.

### Examples of ability

Here are some examples of ability that apply to the above definitions:

- Research

How we find information, collect, analyze and interpret it.

- Problem solving

How we handle challenges and find solutions in difficult moments.

- Art

How we create art in any form. From photography to drawing or sculpting.

- Craft

How we use our manual abilities to create something from very little or sometimes nothing.

- Public speaking

The talent of effectively addressing a room - some people naturally have this from the first day of their lives.

- Negotiation

How to effectively communicate between two parties that have differing views to see a common ground.

## Skills vs abilities

We have seen what both an ability and a skill is and practical examples earlier in the guide. Here are some other ways to interpret their differences.

- Abilities are natural or innate while skills are learned or acquired

E.g. You’re tall and athletic with good hand to eye coordination but you have the skills to play basketball.

- An ability is defined as the capability to do something - while skill can be defined as the ability to do something well.

E.g. The ability to run - and the skill to run fast or a long distance.

- Ability simply refers to the potential of a person to do something. On the other hand, skill refers to the potential possessed by an individual to do something exceptionally well.

E.g. You’re a good artist but you practice a specific form of art that yields results beyond what your natural ability has been able to provide up to that point.

Employers can gain a lot from understanding this clear difference. With skills, they can be learned and used to identify gaps that training and mentoring can help to develop and resolve whilst abilities are innate. A candidate or an employee may have abilities that can be tapped into and used, for example, presentation abilities or negotiation that can come in handy. Therefore the benefits in being able to determine a person’s innate abilities which can be developed into valuable skills are plentiful.

Importantly, an employee can learn about their employees and candidates by focusing on their abilities and helping them to develop their skills.

## Assess skills and abilities with Thomas

Understanding skills, abilities and knowledge is fundamental in the determination of staff training and development needs. Being able to recognize where there are skills and ability gaps will help employers harness strengths and align staff with relevant roles and equally, avoid placing them in roles to which they are not suited.

The Thomas Aptitude assessment can provide a clear distinction of a candidate’s abilities and skills. Measuring an individual's aptitude in 5 key areas Reasoning, Perceptual Speed, Number Speed & Accuracy, Word Meaning and Spatial Visualization), the assessment gives an insight into whether they have the capacity to adapt to new challenges, and if they would be suited to drive change through your organization.

body:
#
Which Personality Attributes are Most Important in the Workplace

8 minutes |

Updated
27 June 2025

By
William Beaumont-Oates

Personality attributes are the individual characteristics and traits that define a person's behaviour, emotions, and thought patterns. In the workplace, personality attributes play an important role in determining job performance, relationships with colleagues, and overall work environment. Understanding and identifying personality attributes in the workplace is essential for creating a positive and productive work environment.

Personality attributes can impact hiring decisions and career progression, as they determine how an individual interacts with others and approaches their work. Employers may use personality assessments as part of their hiring process to identify candidates who possess the necessary attributes for success in a particular role. Additionally, understanding an employee's personality attributes can help managers to provide tailored feedback and development opportunities to support career progression.

Understanding personality attributes is vital for building strong relationships with colleagues, improving job performance, and achieving long-term success in the workplace. In this blog, we’ll look at the personality traits that are most important in the workplace.

## The 'Big Five' personality traits

The Big Five Personality Traits model is a widely used and accepted model for measuring personality traits. It proposes that there are five broad dimensions of personality that can be used to describe individual differences. These traits are openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness, and neuroticism.

### Curiosity

Openness to experience refers to a person's willingness to try new things, seek out new experiences, and engage in creative or intellectual pursuits. This trait is associated with curiosity, imagination, and a desire for variety.

### Conscientiousness

Conscientiousness is characterised by a person's degree of responsibility, dependability, and organisation. People who are high in conscientiousness tend to be diligent, reliable, and focused on achieving their goals.

### Extraversion

Extraversion is a trait that reflects a person's sociability, assertiveness, and energy level. Extraverts tend to be outgoing, talkative, and enjoy being around other people.

### Agreeableness

Agreeableness refers to a person's level of kindness, empathy, and desire to get along with others. Individuals who are high in agreeableness tend to be cooperative, compassionate, and willing to compromise.

### Neuroticism

Neuroticism is a trait that reflects a person's emotional stability and tendency to experience negative emotions such as anxiety, sadness, and anger. People who score high in neuroticism are more likely to experience stress and worry and may have difficulty managing their emotions.

## ’The history of the 'Big 5': What are personality attributes?

The Big Five Personality Traits model originated in the 1960s and 1970s as a way to describe and categorise personality traits. Over time, the model has been refined and is now widely accepted and used in personality research. Each of the five traits can manifest in different ways in the workplace. For example, an employee who scores high in conscientiousness may be punctual, detail-oriented, and reliable, while an employee who scores high in extraversion may be outgoing, sociable, and enjoy teamwork.

The Big Five Personality Traits model is related to other personality models and frameworks, such as the Myers-Briggs Type Indicator and the HEXACO model. However, the Big Five is considered to be more scientifically robust and comprehensive than other models.

Understanding personality traits is important when it comes to hiring, team building, and employee development. By using personality assessments, employers can identify candidates who have the necessary personality traits for a particular role or team. This can help to reduce turnover and improve job satisfaction. In addition, understanding personality traits can help managers to build stronger teams by matching individuals with complementary traits and providing targeted development opportunities.

There are several ways to measure or assess the Big Five Personality Traits in the workplace. The High Potential Trait Indicator developed by psychologists Dr Adrian Furnham and Ian MacRae measures the five facets of the model. However, behavioural and peer assessments can also be effective. It's important to note that while personality assessments can be useful, they should be used in conjunction with other selection criteria to make hiring decisions.

## Personality attributes for jobs: how characteristics affect performance

Studies show that personality can affect all aspects of a person’s performance and behaviour, from how someone deals with stress to their communication preferences. Personality can affect work performance by influencing how an individual behaves, interacts with others, and approaches their work tasks. High functioning organisations know how to unlock their people’s potential, capabilities and inner sense of motivation. By doing so, they make productivity, innovation and performance gains that of them ahead of the competition. Here are some examples of how personality traits can affect the workplace:

### 1. Conscientiousness

People who are more conscientious will regularly plan ahead and analyse their own behaviour to see how it affects others. This trait has consistently been shown to be the biggest predictor of workplace success, besides sociological factors such as access to opportunity.

### 2. Curiosity

Someone who scores highly for ‘openness’ is more likely to think creatively, be inquisitive and inclined to seek new adventures. They are also more likely to embrace change and the alternative perspectives that fuel innovation.

### 3. Extraversion

Studies show that people who are climbing the career ladder are more outgoing. These individuals may become less motivated over time in remote working contexts or roles where they are shut away from other people.

### 4. Agreeableness

People who are more agreeable are strong team players, however they may be less comfortable with interpersonal conflict than others and can lack assertion. Perhaps because of this, high agreeableness is negatively correlated with leadership.

### 5. Neuroticism

People who have higher levels of neuroticism tend to be less self-confident and may be inclined to worry. Those who are lower in neuroticism are generally more relaxed and even tempered, and studies show that leaders are typically lower in this trait.

It is important to note that while personality traits can provide valuable insights into how an individual may perform in certain roles, they are not the sole determinant of work performance and should be used in conjunction with other factors such as skills, experience, and qualifications. When an employer understands different personality types they can better manage individuals to help them overcome challenges, improve productivity and help them to achieve their potential within the organisation.

## Common examples of personality attribute

A great employee is someone who understands their role with a company and interacts well with their supervisors and co-workers. An ideal employee who complements their team’s skills and personalities, and whose internal motivations align with the organisational goals and ambitions. The traits of a great employee are linked to their personality and approach to their responsibilities. Let’s take a look at some of these qualities.

### Reliability

Reliable employees are an essential component of any successful business. Their punctuality, consistency, and ability to meet deadlines are critical factors that contribute to their reliability. Punctual employees show professionalism and respect for their colleagues, managers, and clients, while consistent employees provide stability and predictability to the workplace. Meeting deadlines demonstrates responsibility, organisation, and time-management skills, all of which are highly valued by employers. Ultimately, reliable employees form the backbone of an organisation, and their contributions are crucial for the smooth running and success of the business.

### Leadership

Leadership qualities are important for all employees, not just managers, as they allow individuals to take ownership of their work and inspire others around them. Employees with leadership skills are able to take initiative, think critically, and solve problems independently, which can help to streamline processes and improve productivity. These individuals are able to motivate and encourage their colleagues to perform at their best, which can help to create a positive and collaborative work environment. By exhibiting leadership qualities, employees can demonstrate their value to the organisation and position themselves for career growth and advancement opportunities. Ultimately, leadership skills are essential for all employees as they enable individuals to contribute to the success of the business and make a meaningful impact on the organisation as a whole.

### Self-reliance

Self-reliance is a crucial trait for employees to possess, particularly when it comes to problem-solving and decision-making. Self-reliant employees take responsibility for their own work and are not afraid to take the initiative when necessary. They are able to identify and address issues independently, without relying on others to guide them. This can help to increase productivity and reduce the need for micromanagement. Self-reliant employees are also able to make decisions confidently, without waiting for approval or direction from superiors. This can help to improve efficiency and streamline processes. Ultimately, self-reliance is an important trait for employees to have, as it demonstrates accountability and autonomy, which are highly valued by employers.

### Honesty

Honest employees play a crucial role in fostering a positive work environment by building trust with their colleagues and customers. Their honesty demonstrates a commitment to integrity and ethics, which in turn fosters an environment of trust and transparency. This environment is essential for collaboration and effective teamwork, as well as for building strong relationships with customers. Honesty is also a core value that is highly valued by all employers, as it allows for greater transparency, accountability, and reliability in the workplace. Overall, honest employees are a vital asset to any workplace, as they promote a culture of trust and ethical behaviour, which is essential for the success of any organisation.

### Ambition

Ambitious employees are highly driven individuals who are motivated to achieve their goals and often exceed expectations. They possess a strong desire to succeed and are constantly looking for ways to improve their skills and knowledge. This drive and determination often result in them taking on additional responsibilities and going above and beyond what is expected of them. They are self-motivated and always seeking out new challenges to enhance their skills and advance their careers. Ambitious employees are valued by employers as they bring a sense of energy and enthusiasm to the workplace and are instrumental in driving the organisation towards success. Their passion and dedication inspire others around them and set a high standard for the entire team.

### Creativity

Creativity is a valuable trait that is essential in many different industries and job roles. Employees who think creatively are often able to see problems from different perspectives and come up with innovative solutions that others may not have considered. This ability to think outside the box can be particularly valuable in industries where disruption and change are frequent, such as technology or marketing. Creativity can also help employees to develop new products, services, and strategies that can give their company a competitive edge. By bringing fresh ideas to the table, creative employees can help their company stay ahead of the competition and adapt to changing market conditions.

### Self-awareness

Self-awareness is an important trait for employees to possess as it allows them to understand their strengths and weaknesses and work effectively with others. Self-aware employees are able to identify areas where they need improvement and take steps to develop their skills. This awareness can also help them to understand how they are perceived by others and adjust their behaviour accordingly, which is important in team settings. Self-aware employees are also more receptive to feedback and criticism, as they are able to see these comments constructively, as opportunities for growth and development. They are able to take feedback objectively and use it to improve their performance. By understanding themselves and their impact on others, self-aware employees are able to build stronger relationships with their colleagues and work more effectively as part of a team.

### Tenacity and dedication

Tenacity and dedication are important traits for employees to possess, particularly when faced with challenging tasks or projects. Dedicated employees are committed to their work and are willing to put in extra effort to achieve their goals. They are persistent in the face of obstacles and are not easily discouraged by setbacks or failures. This determination and perseverance enable them to overcome difficult challenges and achieve success. Dedicated employees often go the extra mile to ensure that their work is completed to the best of their ability and are willing to put in extra time and effort to meet deadlines. This level of commitment is highly valued by employers as it demonstrates a strong work ethic and a willingness to take responsibility for one's work.

### Collaboration and teamwork

Collaboration and teamwork are essential for most workplaces as they enable employees to work together towards common goals and achieve success. Employees who are good team players are able to work well with others, share their knowledge and expertise, and help their colleagues succeed. They understand that the success of the team is just as important as individual success and are willing to put in the effort to ensure that the team achieves its goals. Good team players are also effective communicators, able to listen actively and express their thoughts and ideas clearly. They are adaptable and flexible, able to work with a variety of personalities and adapt to changing circumstances. In addition, they are supportive of their colleagues and work collaboratively to achieve success.

### Communication

Communication is a vital skill for employees to possess in any job role as it enables them to express themselves clearly, listen actively, and build strong relationships with their colleagues and customers. Employees who are good communicators are able to articulate their thoughts and ideas clearly, convey information effectively, and listen attentively to the needs and concerns of others. They are skilled in both verbal and written communication, able to adapt their communication style to suit the needs of different audiences. Good communicators also understand the importance of building strong relationships with their colleagues and customers, and are able to do so through effective communication. They are able to build rapport, establish trust, and work collaboratively towards common goals.

##

## Which personality traits are most valuable to employers

Personality traits play an important role in an individual's success at work, and studies show that personality is more predictive of professional effectiveness than previous experience (Furnham). The Thomas Personality assessment was explicitly developed to measure the traits that correlate most strongly with professional success.

Studies and analysis of large datasets show that conscientiousness – which involves being dependable, persevering, and orderly– is the most predictive of academic and professional success and is also the most highly sought after personality attribute in employees. Conscientious people are self-disciplined, organised, deliberate, and have a need for achievement. They characteristically arrive on time, are focused on completing their tasks, and are helpful to their co-workers. Perhaps counterintuitively, one study found that conscientious people "have fewer strokes, lower blood pressure, and a lower incidence of Alzheimer's disease."

Agreeableness – which indicates cooperative behaviour as well as being flexible and tolerant, has been shown to be the second most valued personality trait among employers. This personality trait refers to an individual's ability to work well with others and be cooperative and supportive in a team setting. Agreeable employees are often empathetic, kind, and easy to get along with, which can lead to improved communication and collaboration within the workplace.

At the bottom end of personality hierarchies, emotional intelligence is a crucial trait for workplace success, and is especially important for people managers and leaders. The inverse of neuroticism, an emotionally intelligent person will typically be better able to manage their emotions and those of others and remain calm in high-pressure work environments, helping teams to push through adversity to achieve results.

In our fast paced and competitive market, openness to experience is increasingly important. This personality trait is characterised by a willingness to try new things and explore new ideas. Employees who are open to experience tend to be creative, curious, and adaptable, helping organisations to innovate to stay competitive and respond in an agile way to constantly evolving business environments.

## Personality: predicting professional success

Discovering different personality types can help organisations to optimise workforce efficacy and productivity, improving people metrics across the board and ultimately elevating company performance. Understanding which of the personality attributes that are most important in the workplace, in different teams and environments can help leading organisations get ahead. Behavioral assessments reveal how individuals communicate, influence others, and respond to pressure in the workplace. These insights help organisations identify leadership potential early and strengthen succession planning.

Behavioral assessments focus on how individuals are likely to act in a work environment, such as communication style and pace of work. Personality assessments measure underlying traits and preferences. Used together, they provide a more complete view of workplace performance.

### How can behavioral assessments support leadership development programmes?

Behavioral assessments provide insight into how leaders communicate, motivate others, and respond to challenges. This enables organisations to tailor development programmes to individual needs and improve leadership effectiveness.

#
Psychometric Testing in Recruitment: A Complete Guide

14 minutes |

Updated
10 July 2026

By
Caitlin Meyer

Psychometric testing in recruitment helps employers make more consistent, objective hiring decisions by assessing cognitive ability, workplace behaviors, personality traits and emotional intelligence. Used alongside interviews and CV screening, psychometric assessments can improve hiring accuracy, reduce bias and help organizations identify candidates with strong long-term potential.

Hiring decisions are rarely straightforward. A candidate might interview confidently, but struggle to collaborate under pressure. Another may have the right technical background on paper, yet lack the communication style or behavioral traits needed to succeed within a particular team. That’s one reason psychometric testing in recruitment has become a standard part of modern hiring processes across many organizations.

Psychometric assessments give hiring teams additional insight into how candidates think, communicate and work. Rather than relying solely on CVs, interviews or instinct, employers can introduce more structured and objective ways to assess suitability for a role. From aptitude and personality assessments to behavioral and emotional intelligence testing, these tools help organizations make more informed recruitment decisions while improving hiring consistency across teams and managers.

In this guide, we’ll explore how psychometric tests in recruitment can be used, the different assessment types available, the benefits and limitations of psychometric testing, and how organizations can implement assessments effectively within their hiring process.

## What is Psychometric Testing in Recruitment?

Psychometric testing in recruitment refers to the use of scientifically designed assessments to evaluate a candidate's cognitive abilities, personality traits, workplace behaviors and emotional intelligence. Employers use psychometric tests alongside interviews, CV screening and other assessment methods to gain more objective insights into candidate suitability.

These assessments help organizations evaluate qualities that can be difficult to measure through traditional recruitment methods alone, including problem-solving ability, communication style, behavioral tendencies and leadership potential. When used as part of a structured hiring process, psychometric testing can improve hiring consistency and support more informed recruitment decisions.

## Why Employers Use Psychometric Tests

Organizations are under increasing pressure to make hiring decisions that are both efficient and defensible. As recruitment volumes grow and hiring responsibilities become more distributed across managers, consistency becomes harder to maintain. Psychometric testing helps introduce a more structured framework for assessing candidates against the requirements of a role.

For many employers, the biggest challenge is evaluating the qualities that influence long-term performance and team success. Communication style, problem-solving ability, adaptability and behavioral fit are often far more difficult to assess through CVs and interviews alone.

Psychometric recruitment provides additional insight into how candidates are likely to operate within a working environment. Depending on the assessment type, organizations can evaluate:

- Cognitive ability and learning agility

- Workplace behaviors and communication preferences

- Leadership potential

- Emotional intelligence and self-awareness

- Decision-making style

- Alignment with team dynamics or role requirements

This becomes particularly valuable in recruitment scenarios where consistency matters at scale. Examples of how psychometric testing supports hiring:

Recruitment challengeHow psychometric testing supports hiring

Multiple hiring managers assessing candidates differentlyCreates a more standardised assessment framework.

High-volume recruitment campaignsHelps screen candidates more efficiently and consistently.

Leadership hiringIdentifies behavioral and personality indicators linked to leadership effectiveness.

Customer-facing rolesAssesses communication style, resilience and interpersonal strengths.

Technical or specialist hiringSupports evaluation of reasoning ability and problem-solving capability.

Internal mobility and succession planningHelps identify long-term development and leadership potential.

For HR leaders and talent teams, another advantage is hiring alignment across the organization. Structured assessments create a shared evaluation framework, helping reduce subjective decision-making between departments or hiring managers. This is particularly important for growing organizations where recruitment processes need to remain consistent as teams scale.

When integrated effectively alongside interviews and structured hiring processes, psychometric assessments can support:

- More informed hiring decisions

- Better candidate-role alignment

- Improved hiring consistency

- Reduced bias within assessment processes

- Stronger onboarding and development planning

- Greater confidence in long-term hiring decisions

Many organizations also use psychometric assessments beyond recruitment alone. Insights gathered during hiring can later support onboarding, leadership development and employee progression initiatives, creating longer-term value from the assessment process.

Different assessment types often work best in combination. For example, a leadership recruitment process may include cognitive testing alongside personality and emotional intelligence assessments to provide a broader view of decision-making capability, communication style and leadership potential.

### Aptitude Tests

Aptitude tests assess cognitive ability and are commonly used to evaluate how effectively candidates process information, solve problems and learn new concepts. These assessments are particularly valuable in recruitment scenarios where reasoning ability, learning agility or information processing speed are closely linked to performance.

Many organizations use aptitude tests within:

- Graduate recruitment programmes

- Technical and analytical hiring

- High-volume recruitment campaigns

- Roles requiring rapid decision-making or complex problem-solving

Common aptitude test categories include:

- Numerical reasoning

- Verbal reasoning

- Logical reasoning

- Abstract or inductive reasoning

- Error checking and attention to detail

For employers, aptitude testing introduces a more objective way to compare candidates consistently, particularly where CV experience alone may not fully indicate future capability or potential.

Within recruitment processes, aptitude assessments are often combined with interviews and behavioral assessments to create a broader picture of candidate suitability. Thomas’ Aptitude Assessments support organizations looking to evaluate cognitive capability as part of structured hiring processes.

### Personality Tests

Personality assessments explore the traits, preferences and workplace tendencies that influence how individuals approach their work, interact with others and respond to different professional environments.

Within recruitment, personality testing is often used to support hiring decisions where communication style, leadership capability, adaptability or team dynamics are particularly important. Unlike aptitude testing, which focuses on cognitive ability, personality assessments provide insight into behavioral preferences and working style.

This can help employers evaluate factors such as:

- Approach to collaboration and teamwork

- Communication and influencing style

- Response to pressure or ambiguity

- Motivation and decision-making tendencies

- Leadership and management potential

- Alignment with role demands or organizational culture

For example, a highly autonomous technical role may require different behavioral characteristics than a customer-facing leadership position. Personality assessments help organizations assess these distinctions more consistently during recruitment.

They can also improve the quality of hiring conversations. Assessment insights often provide interviewers with more targeted areas to explore, creating more structured discussions around communication preferences, working relationships and management style.

Many organizations use personality assessments as part of broader structured hiring frameworks, particularly for:

- Leadership recruitment

- Management succession planning

- Customer-facing roles

- Team-based environments

- Internal mobility and progression decisions

Thomas’ Workplace Personality Assessments are designed to help organizations better understand how individuals are likely to operate within workplace settings and leadership environments.

### Behavioral Assessments

Behavioral assessments focus on how individuals are likely to communicate, respond to challenges and interact within workplace environments. In recruitment, these assessments are commonly used to improve understanding of working style, team dynamics and behavioral fit.

They can help organizations evaluate:

- Communication preferences

- Response to pressure or change

- Pace and decision-making style

- Collaboration and relationship-building tendencies

- Motivators and behavioral drivers

- Preferred working environments

This becomes increasingly important in organizations where hiring consistency matters across multiple teams or managers. Behavioral assessments introduce a more structured way to evaluate workplace fit without relying solely on subjective impressions from interviews.

For example:

- Sales roles may benefit from behavioral profiles linked to influence and resilience

- Operational or process-driven roles may require greater consistency and attention to detail

- Leadership positions often require a balance of communication, adaptability and decision-making capability

Behavioral insights can also support onboarding and team integration after recruitment decisions are made, giving managers a clearer understanding of how new hires prefer to work and communicate.

Thomas’ Behavioral Assessments use DISC-based profiling to help organizations understand behavioral tendencies within workplace contexts.

### Emotional Intelligence Assessments

Emotional intelligence assessments evaluate how effectively individuals recognise, manage and respond to emotions within professional environments. In recruitment, these assessments are often used for roles where communication, leadership and interpersonal effectiveness play a central role in performance.

High emotional intelligence is closely associated with workplace capabilities such as:

- Self-awareness

- Relationship management

- Collaboration

- Conflict resolution

- Empathy and communication

- Adaptability under pressure

For leadership and management recruitment, emotional intelligence can provide additional insight into how candidates may influence teams, handle difficult conversations or navigate organizational change.

These assessments are particularly relevant for:

- Leadership and management roles

- Customer-facing positions

- Team-based environments

- HR and people-focused functions

- Roles requiring high stakeholder interaction

Emotional intelligence assessments are rarely used in isolation. Most organizations combine them with behavioral or personality assessments to create a broader understanding of candidate suitability and leadership potential.

In practice, emotional intelligence insights can also support employee development after hiring. Assessment data may help managers identify communication strengths, coaching opportunities or leadership development priorities over time.

Thomas’ Emotional Intelligence Assessments help organizations evaluate interpersonal effectiveness and workplace communication capabilities within recruitment and development processes.

## Benefits of Psychometric Testing in Recruitment

For organizations managing complex or high-volume hiring, psychometric testing can improve both the quality and consistency of recruitment decisions. Assessments provide structured insight into candidate capability and working style, helping employers evaluate factors that are difficult to assess through interviews and CVs alone.

One of the primary advantages is greater objectivity within the hiring process. Recruitment decisions are often influenced by unconscious bias, interviewer preference or inconsistent evaluation criteria between hiring managers. Psychometric testing introduces a more standardised framework, helping organizations assess candidates against defined competencies and behavioral requirements.

This becomes particularly valuable in growing organizations where hiring responsibilities are shared across multiple teams or departments.

Used effectively, psychometric assessments can support:

- More consistent hiring decisions across managers and teams

- Improved assessment of soft skills and workplace behaviors

- Better alignment between candidates and role requirements

- Reduced reliance on subjective interview impressions

- Faster candidate screening within high-volume recruitment

- Improved onboarding and development planning

- Greater confidence in leadership and succession hiring

Assessments also help organizations identify future potential, not simply immediate suitability. For example, cognitive and behavioral insights may highlight candidates with strong learning agility or leadership capability, even where their previous experience appears less conventional.

From an operational perspective, psychometric testing can support recruitment efficiency. Structured assessments help organizations shortlist candidates more consistently and focus interview stages on higher-quality discussions rather than basic screening.

Assessment insights often even remain valuable after hiring decisions have been made, particularly within:

- Onboarding and team integration

- Leadership development

- Internal mobility

- Coaching and management support

- Succession planning

This creates a more connected approach to talent management across the employee lifecycle.

At the same time, psychometric testing tends to be most effective when used as part of a broader structured hiring process. Assessments should support decision-making rather than replace human evaluation entirely. Combining psychometric insight with structured interviews, role-based assessment and hiring manager expertise typically leads to stronger outcomes than relying on any single recruitment method in isolation.

### Key benefits of psychometric testing in recruitment

- Introduces greater consistency across hiring decisions

- Supports more objective candidate assessment

- Improves evaluation of soft skills and behavioral fit

- Helps identify long-term potential and leadership capability

- Enhances recruitment scalability and efficiency

- Supports onboarding and employee development planning

- Reduces over-reliance on CVs and interview performance

- Creates more structured and defensible hiring processes

## Potential Drawbacks and Limitations of Psychometric Testing

Psychometric testing can strengthen recruitment processes significantly, but assessments are not without limitations. Organizations that rely too heavily on testing, or use assessments without clear hiring frameworks, can create poor candidate experiences and make less effective hiring decisions.

The most effective recruitment strategies treat psychometric testing as one component within a broader assessment process. Interviews, role-based evaluation, experience and managerial judgement still play an important role in understanding candidate suitability.

One common challenge is over-interpreting assessment results. Psychometric tools are designed to provide insight into likely behaviors, preferences or cognitive strengths. They are not definitive predictors of future performance in every situation.

For example:

- A candidate may perform strongly in a behavioral assessment but lack role-specific experience

- High cognitive scores do not automatically translate into effective collaboration or leadership capability

- Personality assessments indicate tendencies rather than fixed behaviors

Context matters. Assessment results should always be interpreted alongside the demands of the role, organizational environment and wider recruitment evidence.

Candidate experience is another important consideration. Lengthy or poorly explained testing processes can reduce engagement, particularly within competitive hiring markets where candidates are evaluating employers as much as employers are evaluating them.

Organizations should therefore ensure:

- Assessments are relevant to the role

- Testing stages are proportionate and clearly communicated

- Candidates understand why assessments are being used

- Results are interpreted consistently across hiring managers

- Assessments support fair and inclusive recruitment practices

There are also operational risks where psychometric testing is introduced without sufficient training or structure. Inconsistent interpretation between managers can undermine the objectivity these assessments are designed to support.

## When Should Companies Use Psychometric Testing?

Psychometric testing becomes increasingly valuable as organizations face greater complexity within recruitment. For smaller businesses hiring occasionally, informal hiring processes may appear manageable. As organizations grow, however, inconsistency between hiring decisions often becomes more visible.

Different managers assess candidates differently. Interview quality varies. Hiring criteria become less defined across departments. Over time, this can affect performance, retention, team dynamics and leadership quality.

Structured assessment frameworks help address these challenges by creating more consistent approaches to candidate evaluation.

Psychometric testing is particularly useful when organizations are:

- Scaling recruitment across multiple teams or regions

- Hiring for leadership or management positions

- Recruiting at volume

- Experiencing inconsistent hiring outcomes

- Looking to improve candidate-role alignment

- Building succession or internal mobility strategies

- Standardising hiring processes across managers

- Recruiting for roles where communication, adaptability or behavioral fit strongly influence performance

For example, a growing organization may initially rely heavily on hiring manager instinct and interview performance. As hiring volume increases, this often creates variability in recruitment quality between departments. Psychometric assessments can help establish more consistent evaluation criteria across the business.

Leadership recruitment is another common use case. Senior hires often influence organizational culture, team performance and long-term business outcomes far beyond their immediate role responsibilities. Behavioral, personality and emotional intelligence assessments can provide additional insight into leadership style, communication tendencies and decision-making approaches.

Psychometric testing also supports recruitment in environments where technical capability alone is insufficient. Customer-facing, management and collaborative roles frequently require strong interpersonal effectiveness alongside functional expertise.

Many organizations additionally introduce psychometric assessments when:

- Employee turnover becomes a recurring issue

- Teams struggle with communication or collaboration

- Hiring managers lack confidence in interview-only hiring decisions

- Internal progression pathways need greater structure

- Recruitment processes become difficult to scale consistently

Importantly, psychometric testing tends to deliver the greatest value when integrated within broader structured recruitment processes. Organizations that define clear role requirements, assessment criteria and interview frameworks are typically better positioned to use psychometric insight effectively.

## How to Implement Psychometric Testing in Recruitment

Assessment data is most valuable when it supports clearly defined hiring objectives, role requirements and decision-making frameworks. Without that structure, psychometric testing can become inconsistent across teams and difficult to interpret effectively.

### 1. Define what success looks like for the role

Before introducing assessments, organizations should identify the characteristics most closely linked to success within the role itself.

This may include:

- Cognitive capability and learning agility

- Communication and collaboration style

- Leadership behaviors

- Adaptability and resilience

- Customer-facing strengths

- Attention to detail or analytical reasoning

Different roles require different assessment approaches. A graduate recruitment campaign may prioritise aptitude testing, while leadership hiring may place greater emphasis on behavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Clear role profiling helps ensure assessments remain relevant and proportionate.

### 2. Select assessment types aligned to hiring goals

The most effective psychometric testing recruitment processes use assessment categories selectively rather than applying the same testing model universally.

For example:

Hiring objectiveAssessment types commonly used

Graduate or early-career hiringAptitude and reasoning tests.

Leadership recruitmentPersonality, behavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Customer-facing rolesBehavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Technical or analytical rolesCognitive and aptitude testing.

Team-fit and collaborationBehavioral and personality assessments.

Assessment selection should reflect the practical demands of the role rather than generic hiring preferences.

### 3. Integrate assessments within the wider recruitment process

Psychometric testing tends to work best when integrated alongside structured interviews and role-based evaluation methods.

A common implementation structure may include:

- CV or application screening

- Early-stage psychometric assessment

- Structured interview process

- Role-specific task or scenario assessment

- Final decision-making using combined evidence

This creates a more balanced evaluation framework while reducing over-reliance on any single assessment method.

Assessment insights can also improve interview quality by helping hiring managers explore areas such as communication style, leadership approach or problem-solving tendencies in greater depth.

### 4. Train hiring managers on interpretation and consistency

One of the most common implementation issues is inconsistent interpretation between managers. Psychometric assessments provide indicators and behavioral insight, not fixed conclusions. Without guidance, different hiring managers may draw very different interpretations from the same results.

Organizations should therefore establish:

- Clear assessment interpretation guidance

- Defined scoring or evaluation frameworks

- Structured interview criteria linked to assessment findings

- Consistent hiring processes across teams

This becomes particularly important in larger organizations where recruitment responsibilities are distributed across departments.

### 5. Consider candidate experience carefully

Candidate experience has a direct impact on employer perception and recruitment conversion rates.

Assessment stages should therefore feel:

- Relevant to the role

- Clearly explained

- Appropriate in length

- Professionally integrated within the hiring journey

Poorly positioned or excessive testing can reduce candidate engagement, particularly in competitive hiring markets.

Transparency also matters. Candidates should understand:

- Why assessments are being used

- How results contribute to decision-making

- What the process involves

Organizations that communicate the purpose of assessments clearly often create stronger candidate trust and engagement throughout recruitment.

### 6. Use assessment insight beyond hiring decisions

Psychometric assessments often provide value beyond candidate selection alone.

Many organizations use assessment data to support:

- Onboarding and team integration

- Leadership development

- Coaching conversations

- Internal mobility

- Succession planning

- Communication and management support

This creates greater long-term value from recruitment assessment processes while helping managers support employee development more effectively after hiring.

### Practical implementation checklist

For organizations introducing psychometric testing into recruitment, implementation is typically strongest when:

- Assessments align to role requirements

- Testing supports structured hiring processes

- Managers receive interpretation guidance

- Candidate experience remains proportionate and transparent

- Assessments complement interviews rather than replace them

- Results are applied consistently across teams

- Assessment insights support longer-term talent development

Done well, psychometric testing can strengthen recruitment consistency, improve hiring confidence and create more structured talent decision-making across the organization.

## Choosing the Right Psychometric Test for Your Hiring Process

The effectiveness of psychometric testing depends heavily on selecting assessments that align with the demands of the role and the outcomes the organization is trying to improve.

Different assessments measure different aspects of candidate suitability. Using cognitive testing for a highly relationship-driven leadership role, for example, may provide limited hiring value on its own. Equally, relying solely on personality assessments for technical recruitment may leave important capability gaps within the evaluation process.

For HR and talent leaders, assessment selection should begin with a clear understanding of:

- The behaviors linked to success within the role

- The complexity of the working environment

- The level of collaboration or leadership required

- The importance of learning agility or problem-solving capability

- Existing hiring challenges within the organization

### Matching assessment types to hiring goals

Hiring goalRecommended assessment focus

Graduate and early-career recruitmentAptitude and cognitive ability testing.

Leadership and management hiringPersonality, behavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Customer-facing rolesBehavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Technical or analytical recruitmentNumerical, logical and aptitude testing.

Team-fit and collaborationBehavioral and personality assessments.

Succession planning and internal mobilityPersonality, behavioral and leadership-focused assessments.

In many cases, combining assessment types creates a more balanced evaluation process.

For example:

- A leadership recruitment process may combine behavioral profiling with emotional intelligence assessment

- High-volume graduate hiring may use aptitude testing alongside structured interviews

- Sales recruitment may benefit from behavioral and communication-focused assessments

- Technical hiring may combine cognitive testing with role-based scenario exercises

Assessment choice should also reflect hiring maturity and operational scale. Organizations hiring across multiple departments or regions often benefit from broader structured assessment frameworks that improve consistency between managers and recruitment teams.

From a candidate experience perspective, relevance matters as well. Assessments should feel connected to the responsibilities and expectations of the role rather than appearing generic or excessive.

When implemented strategically, psychometric testing can help organizations create recruitment processes that are more structured, scalable and evidence-informed without losing the human judgement that remains essential within hiring decisions.

## Common Mistakes When Using Psychometric Testing

Psychometric testing can strengthen recruitment processes considerably, but poor implementation often limits its effectiveness. Many of the challenges associated with psychometric testing come less from the assessments themselves and more from how organizations apply and interpret them.

### Over-relying on assessment results

Psychometric assessments are designed to indicate likely tendencies and strengths, not guarantee future performance.

Problems can arise when organizations:

- Treat assessment scores as absolute pass/fail criteria

- Ignore wider contextual factors such as experience or role complexity

- Use assessments to eliminate candidates too early in the process

- Prioritise “ideal profiles” over practical capability and diversity of thinking

Strong hiring decisions usually come from combining multiple evidence sources rather than relying heavily on a single assessment outcome.

### Using the wrong assessments for the role

Different roles require different assessment approaches. Applying generic testing across all recruitment activities can reduce relevance and create poor candidate experiences.

For example:

- Leadership hiring often benefits from behavioral and emotional intelligence assessments

- Technical recruitment may require stronger cognitive or aptitude evaluation

- Customer-facing roles may place greater emphasis on communication and interpersonal capability

Assessment selection should always reflect the practical demands of the role.

### Inconsistent interpretation between hiring managers

Psychometric testing can improve recruitment consistency, but only when organizations apply assessment frameworks consistently across teams.

Without clear guidance:

- Managers may interpret results differently

- Hiring standards can become inconsistent

- Bias may re-enter the decision-making process

- Assessment value becomes diluted

Structured interpretation guidance and interviewer training are often critical to successful implementation.

### Creating an excessive testing process

Lengthy or poorly integrated assessment journeys can negatively affect candidate engagement.

Candidates are more likely to disengage when:

- Testing feels repetitive or irrelevant

- Assessment stages are too time-intensive

- The purpose of testing is unclear

- Recruitment timelines become unnecessarily prolonged

This is particularly important within competitive hiring markets where candidate experience directly influences employer perception.

### Failing to connect assessments to broader talent strategy

Many organizations limit psychometric insights to recruitment decisions alone.

In practice, assessment data can also support:

- Onboarding

- Leadership development

- Team integration

- Internal mobility

- Coaching and management support

Without this longer-term application, organizations often miss a significant portion of the value psychometric testing can provide.

### Common implementation mistakes to avoid

- Using psychometric testing in isolation

- Applying generic assessments to every role

- Over-interpreting assessment results

- Failing to train hiring managers on interpretation

- Creating excessive or poorly explained testing stages

- Ignoring candidate experience considerations

- Treating assessments as replacement tools for interviews

- Failing to align testing with wider hiring strategy

For HR and talent leaders, the strongest outcomes usually come from balanced implementation. Psychometric testing works most effectively when integrated thoughtfully within structured, evidence-informed recruitment processes.

## How Psychometric Testing Supports Onboarding and Employee Development

The value of psychometric testing often extends well beyond the hiring decision itself. Assessment insights can help organizations support onboarding, improve team integration and create more targeted employee development strategies over time. When applied effectively, psychometric insight can support wider workforce planning and employee development initiatives across the organization.

### Supporting more effective onboarding

One of the most common challenges after hiring is helping new employees integrate quickly into existing teams and working environments. Psychometric assessments can help managers better understand:

- Communication preferences

- Motivators and behavioral tendencies

- Preferred management styles

- Decision-making approaches

- Areas where additional support may be needed during onboarding

This can improve the quality of early management conversations and help teams adapt more effectively to new working relationships. For example:

- Behavioral insights may help managers tailor communication approaches during onboarding

- Emotional intelligence assessments can support relationship-building within collaborative teams

- Personality assessments may highlight preferred working environments or motivational drivers

Structured onboarding support becomes particularly important for leadership hires, where integration challenges can have a wider organizational impact.

### Improving communication and team dynamics

Psychometric assessments can also help organizations strengthen collaboration within teams. Managers often inherit communication challenges without fully understanding the underlying behavioral differences contributing to them. Assessment insight can help teams identify:

- Differences in communication style

- Preferred ways of working

- Approaches to decision-making

- Responses to pressure or change

This creates more informed discussions around collaboration, management expectations and team effectiveness. In some organizations, behavioral and personality assessments are also used within:

- Team workshops

- Leadership development programmes

- Coaching initiatives

- Conflict resolution support

- Internal mobility planning

### Identifying leadership and development potential

Psychometric testing can also support long-term talent development by helping organizations identify future leadership capability earlier.

Assessment insight may highlight strengths linked to:

- Strategic thinking

- Communication and influence

- Adaptability

- Relationship management

- Decision-making under pressure

- Learning agility

This can support succession planning and help organizations create more structured leadership development pathways.

Importantly, psychometric assessments should not define development potential in isolation. They are most valuable when combined with performance data, managerial observation and ongoing employee feedback.

### Creating a more connected talent strategy

For many organizations, recruitment, onboarding and employee development still operate as separate processes with limited continuity between them. Psychometric assessments can help create stronger alignment across:

- Hiring decisions

- Onboarding support

- Leadership development

- Internal mobility

- Succession planning

- Team effectiveness initiatives

This allows organizations to make greater use of assessment insight throughout the employee lifecycle rather than limiting value to the point of hire alone.

Used strategically, psychometric testing can support more informed people decisions at every stage of workforce development while helping managers better understand how individuals work, communicate and develop over time.

## FAQs

### What is psychometric testing in recruitment?

Psychometric testing in recruitment refers to the use of structured assessments to evaluate a candidate’s cognitive ability, behaviors, personality traits and emotional intelligence during the hiring process. Employers use psychometric assessments to support more objective and consistent hiring decisions alongside interviews, CV screening and other evaluation methods.

### Why do employers use psychometric tests?

Employers use psychometric tests to improve hiring consistency, assess soft skills more effectively and introduce greater objectivity into recruitment decisions. They are particularly useful in high-volume recruitment, leadership hiring and organizations where multiple hiring managers are involved in candidate assessment.

### What are the different types of psychometric tests?

The main types of psychometric tests used in recruitment include aptitude tests, personality assessments, behavioral assessments, and emotional intelligence assessments

Each assessment category measures different aspects of candidate suitability. Aptitude testing focuses on reasoning and cognitive ability, while behavioral and personality assessments explore workplace communication styles, preferences and interpersonal tendencies.

### Are psychometric tests accurate?

Psychometric tests can provide valuable recruitment insight when they are scientifically validated and used appropriately within structured hiring processes. However, no assessment predicts future performance with complete certainty. Psychometric testing is most effective when combined with interviews, role-based assessment and managerial evaluation rather than used as a standalone hiring method.

### What are the disadvantages of psychometric testing?

Potential disadvantages of psychometric testing include over-reliance on assessment results, poor candidate experience if testing is excessive, inconsistent interpretation between hiring managers, and treating assessments as replacements for interviews

Psychometric testing can become less effective when organizations apply assessments without clear hiring frameworks or sufficient manager training.

### How are psychometric tests used in recruitment?

Psychometric tests are commonly used during candidate screening and evaluation stages within recruitment processes.

Organizations may use assessments to shortlist candidates more consistently, assess reasoning and problem-solving capability, evaluate behavioral and communication styles, support leadership hiring, improve hiring objectivity and identify long-term development potential.

## Conclusion

Psychometric testing has become an increasingly important part of modern recruitment, particularly for organizations looking to improve hiring consistency, assess soft skills more effectively and support more objective decision-making.

Used strategically, psychometric assessments help employers build a broader understanding of candidate suitability beyond CVs and interview performance alone. They can support better hiring alignment, improve recruitment scalability and provide valuable insight into long-term potential and workplace fit.

The strongest outcomes typically come from combining psychometric testing with structured interviews, clear role requirements and consistent hiring processes. For HR and talent leaders, the value lies in creating recruitment frameworks that are both evidence-informed and practical to apply at scale.

#
How to Foster a Growth Mindset in the Workplace

9 minutes |

Updated
10 July 2026

By
William Beaumont-Oates

From the world of sports to high-performing business stars, the idea of mindset is not a new concept but in today’s fast paced world where business success is just as important as business survival, developing the right mindset across your business and through your staff is essential.

We’ve all experienced the kind of managers who believe that “you either sink or swim” and some of us have been fortunate enough to have managers who believe that “you can constantly learn, grow and adapt to challenges.”

The latter of the two is a manager or potentially a leader who understands the importance of a growth mindset. From psychological studies to business examples all around the world, developing a growth mindset is a key component of not only motivating and engaging your employees, it can deliver results on the bottom line as well.

In this guide we are going to take a closer look at what a growth mindset is, what the main attributes are to a growth mindset, the benefits in the workplace and how to develop a growth mindset in your organisation.

## What is a growth mindset?

A growth mindset is a way of seeing problems and skills gaps that can be overcome with time, patience and development. The term, “growth mindset” was originally coined by Carol Dweck, a psychologist, professor, and researcher at Stanford University, in her 2006 book Mindset: The New Psychology of Success.

At the time of its publication it showed that a person demonstrates a growth mindset when they believe they’re not limited by inherent traits or abilities. Instead, they have the capacity to learn, grow, and improve.

Talent alone does not create success but moreover, it is experience and applied practice that does - these are the ideas behind a growth mindset.

The author Matthew Syed in his book, Bounce, uses the studies from Carol Dweck on growth mindset to dig into the notion of “inherent abilities” and shows throughout his publication that those who have a growth mindset have generally achieved more in their careers than those who have what is termed as a fixed mindset. Even great sportspeople who appear to be naturally gifted are actually more likely to have a growth mindset as they will practise longer, harder and with the correct instruction to overcome obstacles in their chosen sport.

We have touched upon the fixed mindset but what are the differences between a growth and fixed mindset?

## Growth mindset vs fixed mindset

Those with a fixed mindset believe that they are born with traits, talents, and qualities that are “fixed”, and that no course of training or adaptability can change those traits. It is normal for many people to assume that this is the case, that talent and abilities are something of which we are naturally good at or something which we are not.

Those with a fixed mindset generally struggle to change their viewpoints or find it difficult to commit to change, evolve and improve as they are under the impression that no matter what they do, little will change anyway.

In this type of scenario we are not thinking in terms of fixed traits but moreover, a fixed mindset.

On the other hand, there is the growth mindset, which looks at this from a different perspective. Abilities and talent are considered to be something that can be developed through dedication and hard work. Someone with a growth mindset may think, I’m not a great salesman yet because I haven’t put in the hours of practice, like someone who is a great performer.

People with growth mindsets are continuously open to setting new goals, trying new tactics, and improving their skills. As a result, these individuals are engaged in their work.

## Main attributes of a growth mindset environment

In order to have more individuals in your organisation with a growth mindset, you need to develop the right kind of environment. This means that you must promote the idea that anyone can succeed if they apply the right strategies, work hard and ask for help to improve.

What do the various notable attributes of a growth mindset work environment look like? Here are just a few suggestions.

- Hard work, determination and perseverance are valued over talent

Rather than reward or use language which talks about natural talent, talk about the hard work that has been put into the task and workplace. Reward those who have demonstrated perseverance and determination to complete their goals.

- Employees are helped and encouraged to learn new skills

Setting goals which may be out of reach to begin with can develop employees to try new tactics, evolve their practices and minds and ask those who have achieved them for advice.

- Staff are coached and supported in developing critical thinking skills enabling them to deal with challenging issues

Develop learning resources, have open table discussions, monitor those who need help to learn and grow accordingly.

- Personnel are encouraged to experiment and try new ideas

“No idea is a bad idea” attitude. Test new things, new platforms, ideas, knowledge to overcome obstacles.

- Staff see failures as valuable learning opportunities

Rather than chastise staff who may not have hit the target, positively discuss what can be learnt from the failure and what can be done to turn it into a learning moment for the employee.

- Staff feel empowered and happy to take responsibility for their actions and own up to mistakes

A sure sign that the growth mindset has taken place is when staff openly own up to mistakes as they can see this as a learning opportunity.

- Staff are encouraged to speak up and respect diverse and possibly challenging viewpoints

Nothing is off limits in terms of learning, evolving and growing but equally, viewpoints should be challenged openly and respected.

## Benefits of a growth mindset in the workplace

We need to understand that a growth mindset in the workplace can carry many benefits, and that having individuals with a growth mindset over say, a fixed mindset can make both learning and development within the organisation a better experience for everyone involved. These outcomes can help organisations improve employee performance by encouraging continuous learning and development.

These benefits of having a growth mindset include:

- Improved problem solving

- People with growth mindsets are more likely to see problems as interesting challenges from which they will learn something.

- They will also use lateral thinking as part of their problem solving strategies, picking ideas from different areas because they’re not afraid to try new things.

- Perseverance and tenacity

- People with a growth mindset are more likely to keep on trying and are less likely to give up at the first hurdle.

- Greater creativity

- It is not uncommon to see that a growth mindset and creativity are closely linked.

- Rather than using an idea to say, “I can’t achieve this” a growth mindset will say, “what other ways have I not looked at this issue?” and come up with something “left field” in response.

- Divergent thinking to problem solving increases creativity and equally enhances the growth mindset paradigm.

- Also - creativity can enhance efficiency - which saves money and other resources.

- Change in perspective

- As noted in the comparison between growth and fixed mindsets - the perspective of a growth mindset recognises that growth is about the journey more than the destination.

- Greater trust

- Those with fixed mindsets, who believe their capabilities and those of their workmates are set, are more likely to view colleagues as competitors - not collaborators.

- Corporate cultures rooted in fixed mindsets therefore demonstrate less trust.

- In workplaces with widely shared growth mindsets employees tend to find their workmates more trustworthy.

- Improved staff morale

- Employees at companies with growth mindsets are more likely to feel a strong sense of commitment to the organisation.

- If they see that their opinions are valued their morale and motivation is boosted.

## How to develop a growth mindset in the workplace

The good news is that we can all develop a growth mindset in the workplace. Taking intentional steps to prioritise a growth mindset in the workplace can have major impacts on company culture, performance and workplace relationships which helps with engagement and productivity. Many organisations use these approaches to improve employee performance while creating a more engaged and adaptable workforce.

Here are some suggestions for developing a growth mindset in your workplace:

- Create learning opportunities

- Establish programs that enable staff to learn new skills.

- Consult with staff regarding what they want to learn or know more about.

- Use in house expertise to cross-train between departments.

- Use technology (e.g. mobile based) to deliver training and learning resources in accessible, appealing formats.

- Use the right recruitment messaging

- When hiring - don’t refer to the best and the brightest, talk about opportunities to grow, develop and learn.

- Reward people for their hard work, their strategies, their ability to tackle challenges and for their perseverance.

- Consider both successes and failures as valuable learning opportunities

- Celebrate failures as learning opportunities.

- Encourage a growth mindset in the workplace by celebrating failures as part of the learning process and treating them as a source of valuable data on what worked (and what didn’t).

- Avoid Group Thinking

- It is important to note that a fixed mindset leads to groupthink, a tendency to conform to ideas and beliefs with conservative thinking - which leads to poor decision making.

- Instead, create ways to foster alternative views and constructive criticism.

- Relate staff performance evaluation to learning and not productivity

- Traditional employee performance appraisals might look at levels of output or productivity but, changing this to examine how employees are growing and developing contributes to establishing an organisational growth mindset.

- Encourage and facilitate open and honest sharing

- Leaders with growth mindsets are open to hearing other perspectives, even when they challenge their own.

- Providing the facilities for all employees to make contributions, share ideas and present criticisms contributes to the development of an organisation’s growth mindset.

- Invest in staff development, training and learning

- Companies with growth mindsets know that the full potential of their employees has not yet been realised.

- Describe how investing in upskilling, reskilling, mentoring, coaching and other forms of staff development plays a huge part in establishing a beneficial growth mindset.

## Improving your businesses growth mindset

We all have the ability to learn, grow, evolve and develop. By doing so we can overcome obstacles through time, perseverance and become better employees as well as better people. This is the basis of a growth mindset, and by taking on this vision over something such as a fixed mindset which only looks to reward “inherent ability”, we can create better working conditions and help individuals grow in their role. For more practical guidance, explore the Employee Development Hub.

From better problem solving, more creative thinking and developing trust in the workplace, a growth mindset can be a critical key in your overall success.
