#
Psychometric Testing in Recruitment: A Complete Guide

14 minutes |

Updated
10 July 2026

By
Caitlin Meyer

Psychometric testing in recruitment helps employers make more consistent, objective hiring decisions by assessing cognitive ability, workplace behaviors, personality traits and emotional intelligence. Used alongside interviews and CV screening, psychometric assessments can improve hiring accuracy, reduce bias and help organizations identify candidates with strong long-term potential.

Hiring decisions are rarely straightforward. A candidate might interview confidently, but struggle to collaborate under pressure. Another may have the right technical background on paper, yet lack the communication style or behavioral traits needed to succeed within a particular team. That’s one reason psychometric testing in recruitment has become a standard part of modern hiring processes across many organizations.

Psychometric assessments give hiring teams additional insight into how candidates think, communicate and work. Rather than relying solely on CVs, interviews or instinct, employers can introduce more structured and objective ways to assess suitability for a role. From aptitude and personality assessments to behavioral and emotional intelligence testing, these tools help organizations make more informed recruitment decisions while improving hiring consistency across teams and managers.

In this guide, we’ll explore how psychometric tests in recruitment can be used, the different assessment types available, the benefits and limitations of psychometric testing, and how organizations can implement assessments effectively within their hiring process.

## What is Psychometric Testing in Recruitment?

Psychometric testing in recruitment refers to the use of scientifically designed assessments to evaluate a candidate's cognitive abilities, personality traits, workplace behaviors and emotional intelligence. Employers use psychometric tests alongside interviews, CV screening and other assessment methods to gain more objective insights into candidate suitability.

These assessments help organizations evaluate qualities that can be difficult to measure through traditional recruitment methods alone, including problem-solving ability, communication style, behavioral tendencies and leadership potential. When used as part of a structured hiring process, psychometric testing can improve hiring consistency and support more informed recruitment decisions.

## Why Employers Use Psychometric Tests

Organizations are under increasing pressure to make hiring decisions that are both efficient and defensible. As recruitment volumes grow and hiring responsibilities become more distributed across managers, consistency becomes harder to maintain. Psychometric testing helps introduce a more structured framework for assessing candidates against the requirements of a role.

For many employers, the biggest challenge is evaluating the qualities that influence long-term performance and team success. Communication style, problem-solving ability, adaptability and behavioral fit are often far more difficult to assess through CVs and interviews alone.

Psychometric recruitment provides additional insight into how candidates are likely to operate within a working environment. Depending on the assessment type, organizations can evaluate:

- Cognitive ability and learning agility

- Workplace behaviors and communication preferences

- Leadership potential

- Emotional intelligence and self-awareness

- Decision-making style

- Alignment with team dynamics or role requirements

This becomes particularly valuable in recruitment scenarios where consistency matters at scale. Examples of how psychometric testing supports hiring:

Recruitment challengeHow psychometric testing supports hiring

Multiple hiring managers assessing candidates differentlyCreates a more standardised assessment framework.

High-volume recruitment campaignsHelps screen candidates more efficiently and consistently.

Leadership hiringIdentifies behavioral and personality indicators linked to leadership effectiveness.

Customer-facing rolesAssesses communication style, resilience and interpersonal strengths.

Technical or specialist hiringSupports evaluation of reasoning ability and problem-solving capability.

Internal mobility and succession planningHelps identify long-term development and leadership potential.

For HR leaders and talent teams, another advantage is hiring alignment across the organization. Structured assessments create a shared evaluation framework, helping reduce subjective decision-making between departments or hiring managers. This is particularly important for growing organizations where recruitment processes need to remain consistent as teams scale.

When integrated effectively alongside interviews and structured hiring processes, psychometric assessments can support:

- More informed hiring decisions

- Better candidate-role alignment

- Improved hiring consistency

- Reduced bias within assessment processes

- Stronger onboarding and development planning

- Greater confidence in long-term hiring decisions

Many organizations also use psychometric assessments beyond recruitment alone. Insights gathered during hiring can later support onboarding, leadership development and employee progression initiatives, creating longer-term value from the assessment process.

Different assessment types often work best in combination. For example, a leadership recruitment process may include cognitive testing alongside personality and emotional intelligence assessments to provide a broader view of decision-making capability, communication style and leadership potential.

### Aptitude Tests

Aptitude tests assess cognitive ability and are commonly used to evaluate how effectively candidates process information, solve problems and learn new concepts. These assessments are particularly valuable in recruitment scenarios where reasoning ability, learning agility or information processing speed are closely linked to performance.

Many organizations use aptitude tests within:

- Graduate recruitment programmes

- Technical and analytical hiring

- High-volume recruitment campaigns

- Roles requiring rapid decision-making or complex problem-solving

Common aptitude test categories include:

- Numerical reasoning

- Verbal reasoning

- Logical reasoning

- Abstract or inductive reasoning

- Error checking and attention to detail

For employers, aptitude testing introduces a more objective way to compare candidates consistently, particularly where CV experience alone may not fully indicate future capability or potential.

Within recruitment processes, aptitude assessments are often combined with interviews and behavioral assessments to create a broader picture of candidate suitability. Thomas’ Aptitude Assessments support organizations looking to evaluate cognitive capability as part of structured hiring processes.

### Personality Tests

Personality assessments explore the traits, preferences and workplace tendencies that influence how individuals approach their work, interact with others and respond to different professional environments.

Within recruitment, personality testing is often used to support hiring decisions where communication style, leadership capability, adaptability or team dynamics are particularly important. Unlike aptitude testing, which focuses on cognitive ability, personality assessments provide insight into behavioral preferences and working style.

This can help employers evaluate factors such as:

- Approach to collaboration and teamwork

- Communication and influencing style

- Response to pressure or ambiguity

- Motivation and decision-making tendencies

- Leadership and management potential

- Alignment with role demands or organizational culture

For example, a highly autonomous technical role may require different behavioral characteristics than a customer-facing leadership position. Personality assessments help organizations assess these distinctions more consistently during recruitment.

They can also improve the quality of hiring conversations. Assessment insights often provide interviewers with more targeted areas to explore, creating more structured discussions around communication preferences, working relationships and management style.

Many organizations use personality assessments as part of broader structured hiring frameworks, particularly for:

- Leadership recruitment

- Management succession planning

- Customer-facing roles

- Team-based environments

- Internal mobility and progression decisions

Thomas’ Workplace Personality Assessments are designed to help organizations better understand how individuals are likely to operate within workplace settings and leadership environments.

### Behavioral Assessments

Behavioral assessments focus on how individuals are likely to communicate, respond to challenges and interact within workplace environments. In recruitment, these assessments are commonly used to improve understanding of working style, team dynamics and behavioral fit.

They can help organizations evaluate:

- Communication preferences

- Response to pressure or change

- Pace and decision-making style

- Collaboration and relationship-building tendencies

- Motivators and behavioral drivers

- Preferred working environments

This becomes increasingly important in organizations where hiring consistency matters across multiple teams or managers. Behavioral assessments introduce a more structured way to evaluate workplace fit without relying solely on subjective impressions from interviews.

For example:

- Sales roles may benefit from behavioral profiles linked to influence and resilience

- Operational or process-driven roles may require greater consistency and attention to detail

- Leadership positions often require a balance of communication, adaptability and decision-making capability

Behavioral insights can also support onboarding and team integration after recruitment decisions are made, giving managers a clearer understanding of how new hires prefer to work and communicate.

Thomas’ Behavioral Assessments use DISC-based profiling to help organizations understand behavioral tendencies within workplace contexts.

### Emotional Intelligence Assessments

Emotional intelligence assessments evaluate how effectively individuals recognise, manage and respond to emotions within professional environments. In recruitment, these assessments are often used for roles where communication, leadership and interpersonal effectiveness play a central role in performance.

High emotional intelligence is closely associated with workplace capabilities such as:

- Self-awareness

- Relationship management

- Collaboration

- Conflict resolution

- Empathy and communication

- Adaptability under pressure

For leadership and management recruitment, emotional intelligence can provide additional insight into how candidates may influence teams, handle difficult conversations or navigate organizational change.

These assessments are particularly relevant for:

- Leadership and management roles

- Customer-facing positions

- Team-based environments

- HR and people-focused functions

- Roles requiring high stakeholder interaction

Emotional intelligence assessments are rarely used in isolation. Most organizations combine them with behavioral or personality assessments to create a broader understanding of candidate suitability and leadership potential.

In practice, emotional intelligence insights can also support employee development after hiring. Assessment data may help managers identify communication strengths, coaching opportunities or leadership development priorities over time.

Thomas’ Emotional Intelligence Assessments help organizations evaluate interpersonal effectiveness and workplace communication capabilities within recruitment and development processes.

## Benefits of Psychometric Testing in Recruitment

For organizations managing complex or high-volume hiring, psychometric testing can improve both the quality and consistency of recruitment decisions. Assessments provide structured insight into candidate capability and working style, helping employers evaluate factors that are difficult to assess through interviews and CVs alone.

One of the primary advantages is greater objectivity within the hiring process. Recruitment decisions are often influenced by unconscious bias, interviewer preference or inconsistent evaluation criteria between hiring managers. Psychometric testing introduces a more standardised framework, helping organizations assess candidates against defined competencies and behavioral requirements.

This becomes particularly valuable in growing organizations where hiring responsibilities are shared across multiple teams or departments.

Used effectively, psychometric assessments can support:

- More consistent hiring decisions across managers and teams

- Improved assessment of soft skills and workplace behaviors

- Better alignment between candidates and role requirements

- Reduced reliance on subjective interview impressions

- Faster candidate screening within high-volume recruitment

- Improved onboarding and development planning

- Greater confidence in leadership and succession hiring

Assessments also help organizations identify future potential, not simply immediate suitability. For example, cognitive and behavioral insights may highlight candidates with strong learning agility or leadership capability, even where their previous experience appears less conventional.

From an operational perspective, psychometric testing can support recruitment efficiency. Structured assessments help organizations shortlist candidates more consistently and focus interview stages on higher-quality discussions rather than basic screening.

Assessment insights often even remain valuable after hiring decisions have been made, particularly within:

- Onboarding and team integration

- Leadership development

- Internal mobility

- Coaching and management support

- Succession planning

This creates a more connected approach to talent management across the employee lifecycle.

At the same time, psychometric testing tends to be most effective when used as part of a broader structured hiring process. Assessments should support decision-making rather than replace human evaluation entirely. Combining psychometric insight with structured interviews, role-based assessment and hiring manager expertise typically leads to stronger outcomes than relying on any single recruitment method in isolation.

### Key benefits of psychometric testing in recruitment

- Introduces greater consistency across hiring decisions

- Supports more objective candidate assessment

- Improves evaluation of soft skills and behavioral fit

- Helps identify long-term potential and leadership capability

- Enhances recruitment scalability and efficiency

- Supports onboarding and employee development planning

- Reduces over-reliance on CVs and interview performance

- Creates more structured and defensible hiring processes

## Potential Drawbacks and Limitations of Psychometric Testing

Psychometric testing can strengthen recruitment processes significantly, but assessments are not without limitations. Organizations that rely too heavily on testing, or use assessments without clear hiring frameworks, can create poor candidate experiences and make less effective hiring decisions.

The most effective recruitment strategies treat psychometric testing as one component within a broader assessment process. Interviews, role-based evaluation, experience and managerial judgement still play an important role in understanding candidate suitability.

One common challenge is over-interpreting assessment results. Psychometric tools are designed to provide insight into likely behaviors, preferences or cognitive strengths. They are not definitive predictors of future performance in every situation.

For example:

- A candidate may perform strongly in a behavioral assessment but lack role-specific experience

- High cognitive scores do not automatically translate into effective collaboration or leadership capability

- Personality assessments indicate tendencies rather than fixed behaviors

Context matters. Assessment results should always be interpreted alongside the demands of the role, organizational environment and wider recruitment evidence.

Candidate experience is another important consideration. Lengthy or poorly explained testing processes can reduce engagement, particularly within competitive hiring markets where candidates are evaluating employers as much as employers are evaluating them.

Organizations should therefore ensure:

- Assessments are relevant to the role

- Testing stages are proportionate and clearly communicated

- Candidates understand why assessments are being used

- Results are interpreted consistently across hiring managers

- Assessments support fair and inclusive recruitment practices

There are also operational risks where psychometric testing is introduced without sufficient training or structure. Inconsistent interpretation between managers can undermine the objectivity these assessments are designed to support.

## When Should Companies Use Psychometric Testing?

Psychometric testing becomes increasingly valuable as organizations face greater complexity within recruitment. For smaller businesses hiring occasionally, informal hiring processes may appear manageable. As organizations grow, however, inconsistency between hiring decisions often becomes more visible.

Different managers assess candidates differently. Interview quality varies. Hiring criteria become less defined across departments. Over time, this can affect performance, retention, team dynamics and leadership quality.

Structured assessment frameworks help address these challenges by creating more consistent approaches to candidate evaluation.

Psychometric testing is particularly useful when organizations are:

- Scaling recruitment across multiple teams or regions

- Hiring for leadership or management positions

- Recruiting at volume

- Experiencing inconsistent hiring outcomes

- Looking to improve candidate-role alignment

- Building succession or internal mobility strategies

- Standardising hiring processes across managers

- Recruiting for roles where communication, adaptability or behavioral fit strongly influence performance

For example, a growing organization may initially rely heavily on hiring manager instinct and interview performance. As hiring volume increases, this often creates variability in recruitment quality between departments. Psychometric assessments can help establish more consistent evaluation criteria across the business.

Leadership recruitment is another common use case. Senior hires often influence organizational culture, team performance and long-term business outcomes far beyond their immediate role responsibilities. Behavioral, personality and emotional intelligence assessments can provide additional insight into leadership style, communication tendencies and decision-making approaches.

Psychometric testing also supports recruitment in environments where technical capability alone is insufficient. Customer-facing, management and collaborative roles frequently require strong interpersonal effectiveness alongside functional expertise.

Many organizations additionally introduce psychometric assessments when:

- Employee turnover becomes a recurring issue

- Teams struggle with communication or collaboration

- Hiring managers lack confidence in interview-only hiring decisions

- Internal progression pathways need greater structure

- Recruitment processes become difficult to scale consistently

Importantly, psychometric testing tends to deliver the greatest value when integrated within broader structured recruitment processes. Organizations that define clear role requirements, assessment criteria and interview frameworks are typically better positioned to use psychometric insight effectively.

## How to Implement Psychometric Testing in Recruitment

Assessment data is most valuable when it supports clearly defined hiring objectives, role requirements and decision-making frameworks. Without that structure, psychometric testing can become inconsistent across teams and difficult to interpret effectively.

### 1. Define what success looks like for the role

Before introducing assessments, organizations should identify the characteristics most closely linked to success within the role itself.

This may include:

- Cognitive capability and learning agility

- Communication and collaboration style

- Leadership behaviors

- Adaptability and resilience

- Customer-facing strengths

- Attention to detail or analytical reasoning

Different roles require different assessment approaches. A graduate recruitment campaign may prioritise aptitude testing, while leadership hiring may place greater emphasis on behavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Clear role profiling helps ensure assessments remain relevant and proportionate.

### 2. Select assessment types aligned to hiring goals

The most effective psychometric testing recruitment processes use assessment categories selectively rather than applying the same testing model universally.

For example:

Hiring objectiveAssessment types commonly used

Graduate or early-career hiringAptitude and reasoning tests.

Leadership recruitmentPersonality, behavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Customer-facing rolesBehavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Technical or analytical rolesCognitive and aptitude testing.

Team-fit and collaborationBehavioral and personality assessments.

Assessment selection should reflect the practical demands of the role rather than generic hiring preferences.

### 3. Integrate assessments within the wider recruitment process

Psychometric testing tends to work best when integrated alongside structured interviews and role-based evaluation methods.

A common implementation structure may include:

- CV or application screening

- Early-stage psychometric assessment

- Structured interview process

- Role-specific task or scenario assessment

- Final decision-making using combined evidence

This creates a more balanced evaluation framework while reducing over-reliance on any single assessment method.

Assessment insights can also improve interview quality by helping hiring managers explore areas such as communication style, leadership approach or problem-solving tendencies in greater depth.

### 4. Train hiring managers on interpretation and consistency

One of the most common implementation issues is inconsistent interpretation between managers. Psychometric assessments provide indicators and behavioral insight, not fixed conclusions. Without guidance, different hiring managers may draw very different interpretations from the same results.

Organizations should therefore establish:

- Clear assessment interpretation guidance

- Defined scoring or evaluation frameworks

- Structured interview criteria linked to assessment findings

- Consistent hiring processes across teams

This becomes particularly important in larger organizations where recruitment responsibilities are distributed across departments.

### 5. Consider candidate experience carefully

Candidate experience has a direct impact on employer perception and recruitment conversion rates.

Assessment stages should therefore feel:

- Relevant to the role

- Clearly explained

- Appropriate in length

- Professionally integrated within the hiring journey

Poorly positioned or excessive testing can reduce candidate engagement, particularly in competitive hiring markets.

Transparency also matters. Candidates should understand:

- Why assessments are being used

- How results contribute to decision-making

- What the process involves

Organizations that communicate the purpose of assessments clearly often create stronger candidate trust and engagement throughout recruitment.

### 6. Use assessment insight beyond hiring decisions

Psychometric assessments often provide value beyond candidate selection alone.

Many organizations use assessment data to support:

- Onboarding and team integration

- Leadership development

- Coaching conversations

- Internal mobility

- Succession planning

- Communication and management support

This creates greater long-term value from recruitment assessment processes while helping managers support employee development more effectively after hiring.

### Practical implementation checklist

For organizations introducing psychometric testing into recruitment, implementation is typically strongest when:

- Assessments align to role requirements

- Testing supports structured hiring processes

- Managers receive interpretation guidance

- Candidate experience remains proportionate and transparent

- Assessments complement interviews rather than replace them

- Results are applied consistently across teams

- Assessment insights support longer-term talent development

Done well, psychometric testing can strengthen recruitment consistency, improve hiring confidence and create more structured talent decision-making across the organization.

## Choosing the Right Psychometric Test for Your Hiring Process

The effectiveness of psychometric testing depends heavily on selecting assessments that align with the demands of the role and the outcomes the organization is trying to improve.

Different assessments measure different aspects of candidate suitability. Using cognitive testing for a highly relationship-driven leadership role, for example, may provide limited hiring value on its own. Equally, relying solely on personality assessments for technical recruitment may leave important capability gaps within the evaluation process.

For HR and talent leaders, assessment selection should begin with a clear understanding of:

- The behaviors linked to success within the role

- The complexity of the working environment

- The level of collaboration or leadership required

- The importance of learning agility or problem-solving capability

- Existing hiring challenges within the organization

### Matching assessment types to hiring goals

Hiring goalRecommended assessment focus

Graduate and early-career recruitmentAptitude and cognitive ability testing.

Leadership and management hiringPersonality, behavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Customer-facing rolesBehavioral and emotional intelligence assessments.

Technical or analytical recruitmentNumerical, logical and aptitude testing.

Team-fit and collaborationBehavioral and personality assessments.

Succession planning and internal mobilityPersonality, behavioral and leadership-focused assessments.

In many cases, combining assessment types creates a more balanced evaluation process.

For example:

- A leadership recruitment process may combine behavioral profiling with emotional intelligence assessment

- High-volume graduate hiring may use aptitude testing alongside structured interviews

- Sales recruitment may benefit from behavioral and communication-focused assessments

- Technical hiring may combine cognitive testing with role-based scenario exercises

Assessment choice should also reflect hiring maturity and operational scale. Organizations hiring across multiple departments or regions often benefit from broader structured assessment frameworks that improve consistency between managers and recruitment teams.

From a candidate experience perspective, relevance matters as well. Assessments should feel connected to the responsibilities and expectations of the role rather than appearing generic or excessive.

When implemented strategically, psychometric testing can help organizations create recruitment processes that are more structured, scalable and evidence-informed without losing the human judgement that remains essential within hiring decisions.

## Common Mistakes When Using Psychometric Testing

Psychometric testing can strengthen recruitment processes considerably, but poor implementation often limits its effectiveness. Many of the challenges associated with psychometric testing come less from the assessments themselves and more from how organizations apply and interpret them.

### Over-relying on assessment results

Psychometric assessments are designed to indicate likely tendencies and strengths, not guarantee future performance.

Problems can arise when organizations:

- Treat assessment scores as absolute pass/fail criteria

- Ignore wider contextual factors such as experience or role complexity

- Use assessments to eliminate candidates too early in the process

- Prioritise “ideal profiles” over practical capability and diversity of thinking

Strong hiring decisions usually come from combining multiple evidence sources rather than relying heavily on a single assessment outcome.

### Using the wrong assessments for the role

Different roles require different assessment approaches. Applying generic testing across all recruitment activities can reduce relevance and create poor candidate experiences.

For example:

- Leadership hiring often benefits from behavioral and emotional intelligence assessments

- Technical recruitment may require stronger cognitive or aptitude evaluation

- Customer-facing roles may place greater emphasis on communication and interpersonal capability

Assessment selection should always reflect the practical demands of the role.

### Inconsistent interpretation between hiring managers

Psychometric testing can improve recruitment consistency, but only when organizations apply assessment frameworks consistently across teams.

Without clear guidance:

- Managers may interpret results differently

- Hiring standards can become inconsistent

- Bias may re-enter the decision-making process

- Assessment value becomes diluted

Structured interpretation guidance and interviewer training are often critical to successful implementation.

### Creating an excessive testing process

Lengthy or poorly integrated assessment journeys can negatively affect candidate engagement.

Candidates are more likely to disengage when:

- Testing feels repetitive or irrelevant

- Assessment stages are too time-intensive

- The purpose of testing is unclear

- Recruitment timelines become unnecessarily prolonged

This is particularly important within competitive hiring markets where candidate experience directly influences employer perception.

### Failing to connect assessments to broader talent strategy

Many organizations limit psychometric insights to recruitment decisions alone.

In practice, assessment data can also support:

- Onboarding

- Leadership development

- Team integration

- Internal mobility

- Coaching and management support

Without this longer-term application, organizations often miss a significant portion of the value psychometric testing can provide.

### Common implementation mistakes to avoid

- Using psychometric testing in isolation

- Applying generic assessments to every role

- Over-interpreting assessment results

- Failing to train hiring managers on interpretation

- Creating excessive or poorly explained testing stages

- Ignoring candidate experience considerations

- Treating assessments as replacement tools for interviews

- Failing to align testing with wider hiring strategy

For HR and talent leaders, the strongest outcomes usually come from balanced implementation. Psychometric testing works most effectively when integrated thoughtfully within structured, evidence-informed recruitment processes.

## How Psychometric Testing Supports Onboarding and Employee Development

The value of psychometric testing often extends well beyond the hiring decision itself. Assessment insights can help organizations support onboarding, improve team integration and create more targeted employee development strategies over time. When applied effectively, psychometric insight can support wider workforce planning and employee development initiatives across the organization.

### Supporting more effective onboarding

One of the most common challenges after hiring is helping new employees integrate quickly into existing teams and working environments. Psychometric assessments can help managers better understand:

- Communication preferences

- Motivators and behavioral tendencies

- Preferred management styles

- Decision-making approaches

- Areas where additional support may be needed during onboarding

This can improve the quality of early management conversations and help teams adapt more effectively to new working relationships. For example:

- Behavioral insights may help managers tailor communication approaches during onboarding

- Emotional intelligence assessments can support relationship-building within collaborative teams

- Personality assessments may highlight preferred working environments or motivational drivers

Structured onboarding support becomes particularly important for leadership hires, where integration challenges can have a wider organizational impact.

### Improving communication and team dynamics

Psychometric assessments can also help organizations strengthen collaboration within teams. Managers often inherit communication challenges without fully understanding the underlying behavioral differences contributing to them. Assessment insight can help teams identify:

- Differences in communication style

- Preferred ways of working

- Approaches to decision-making

- Responses to pressure or change

This creates more informed discussions around collaboration, management expectations and team effectiveness. In some organizations, behavioral and personality assessments are also used within:

- Team workshops

- Leadership development programmes

- Coaching initiatives

- Conflict resolution support

- Internal mobility planning

### Identifying leadership and development potential

Psychometric testing can also support long-term talent development by helping organizations identify future leadership capability earlier.

Assessment insight may highlight strengths linked to:

- Strategic thinking

- Communication and influence

- Adaptability

- Relationship management

- Decision-making under pressure

- Learning agility

This can support succession planning and help organizations create more structured leadership development pathways.

Importantly, psychometric assessments should not define development potential in isolation. They are most valuable when combined with performance data, managerial observation and ongoing employee feedback.

### Creating a more connected talent strategy

For many organizations, recruitment, onboarding and employee development still operate as separate processes with limited continuity between them. Psychometric assessments can help create stronger alignment across:

- Hiring decisions

- Onboarding support

- Leadership development

- Internal mobility

- Succession planning

- Team effectiveness initiatives

This allows organizations to make greater use of assessment insight throughout the employee lifecycle rather than limiting value to the point of hire alone.

Used strategically, psychometric testing can support more informed people decisions at every stage of workforce development while helping managers better understand how individuals work, communicate and develop over time.

## FAQs

### What is psychometric testing in recruitment?

Psychometric testing in recruitment refers to the use of structured assessments to evaluate a candidate’s cognitive ability, behaviors, personality traits and emotional intelligence during the hiring process. Employers use psychometric assessments to support more objective and consistent hiring decisions alongside interviews, CV screening and other evaluation methods.

### Why do employers use psychometric tests?

Employers use psychometric tests to improve hiring consistency, assess soft skills more effectively and introduce greater objectivity into recruitment decisions. They are particularly useful in high-volume recruitment, leadership hiring and organizations where multiple hiring managers are involved in candidate assessment.

### What are the different types of psychometric tests?

The main types of psychometric tests used in recruitment include aptitude tests, personality assessments, behavioral assessments, and emotional intelligence assessments

Each assessment category measures different aspects of candidate suitability. Aptitude testing focuses on reasoning and cognitive ability, while behavioral and personality assessments explore workplace communication styles, preferences and interpersonal tendencies.

### Are psychometric tests accurate?

Psychometric tests can provide valuable recruitment insight when they are scientifically validated and used appropriately within structured hiring processes. However, no assessment predicts future performance with complete certainty. Psychometric testing is most effective when combined with interviews, role-based assessment and managerial evaluation rather than used as a standalone hiring method.

### What are the disadvantages of psychometric testing?

Potential disadvantages of psychometric testing include over-reliance on assessment results, poor candidate experience if testing is excessive, inconsistent interpretation between hiring managers, and treating assessments as replacements for interviews

Psychometric testing can become less effective when organizations apply assessments without clear hiring frameworks or sufficient manager training.

### How are psychometric tests used in recruitment?

Psychometric tests are commonly used during candidate screening and evaluation stages within recruitment processes.

Organizations may use assessments to shortlist candidates more consistently, assess reasoning and problem-solving capability, evaluate behavioral and communication styles, support leadership hiring, improve hiring objectivity and identify long-term development potential.

## Conclusion

Psychometric testing has become an increasingly important part of modern recruitment, particularly for organizations looking to improve hiring consistency, assess soft skills more effectively and support more objective decision-making.

Used strategically, psychometric assessments help employers build a broader understanding of candidate suitability beyond CVs and interview performance alone. They can support better hiring alignment, improve recruitment scalability and provide valuable insight into long-term potential and workplace fit.

The strongest outcomes typically come from combining psychometric testing with structured interviews, clear role requirements and consistent hiring processes. For HR and talent leaders, the value lies in creating recruitment frameworks that are both evidence-informed and practical to apply at scale.

#
What is an IQ Test?

6 minutes |

Updated
11 October 2024

By
Caitlin Meyer

IQ assessments have always been a conversation starter as well as a recruitment method. Intelligence Quotient (IQ) was established in the early 1900s as a way to create a standardized measure of intelligence as well as cognitive abilities. Over the years, the IQ test has been used to identify potential leadership material as well those with certain cognitive skills that would go on to be leading names in different fields.

Whilst the legitimacy is still hotly debated, IQ tests have good predictive capacity which shouldn’t be underestimated in some key areas of recruitment and development.

In today’s guide, we are going to take a closer look at IQ tests, what they are, a brief history of the test, how accurate they are and how employers and recruiters can use them (if they should) to help find the right candidate.

## What is IQ?

IQ or Intelligence Quotient is a standard score that shows how far above or below, his/her peer group an individual stands in mental ability. The peer group score is an IQ of 100. The IQ number is attained by giving the same test to huge numbers of people from all socio-economic strata of society and then taking the average.

Coined in 1912 by psychologist William Stern, IQ was represented as a ratio of “mental age to chronological age x 100”. For example if someone was 10 years old and had the mental age of a 10 year old, their IQ would be 100. But if their mental age was for example, 13 rather than 10, their IQ would be 130.

## What are IQ tests?

A typical IQ test consists of taking various tests measuring intelligence including; spatial recognition, short-term memory, mathematical ability, and analytical thinking. Commonly misunderstood as something that tests all the knowledge you have acquired over the years, the IQ test is actually testing your capacity to learn.

The modern day IQ test has come a long way since its inception in the early 20th century. Their purpose hasn’t changed, and the methodology remains similar - in that they are testing facets of an individual’s intelligence quotient rather than anything that has been learned in the past.

There have been several iterations of the IQ test with the most commonly used one being the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS). This was created in 1955 which deviated from previous IQ tests looking at different mental abilities such as verbal, numerical, spatial and logical intelligence. Since its inception, there has been an update to this test, the WAIS-IV.

WAIS-IV contains 10 subtests, along with five supplemental tests. The test provides scores in four major areas of intelligence: a verbal comprehension scale, a perceptual reasoning scale, a working memory scale, and a processing speed scale. An individual is then tested across a group of their peers to provide a more accurate scoring system with two-thirds of scores lying in the normal range between 85 and 115.

## What does an IQ test measure?

An IQ test measures a range of an individual's cognitive ability and provides a score that is intended to serve as a way to measure an individual’s capabilities and potential.

A typical IQ test takes one to two hours and consists of anywhere between 25 and 50 multiple choice questions. It depends on the association administering the test but examinations can be shorter. Tests taken on social media for example can be short but do not cover a wide range of requirements to accurately measure IQ.

## A brief history of IQ tests

The first IQ tests were developed in the late 19th century by Paul Broca (1824-1880) and Sir Francis Galton who were interested in finding a way to standardize the method of measuring intelligence.

Interestingly they thought that they could do this by measuring the human skull, the larger - the more intelligent. Luckily, we moved on from this assumption in the early 20th century when Alfred Binet and Theodore Simon put their minds together to create a better way of measuring intelligence.

Employed by the French ministry of education, the scientists were tasked with finding a way to understand who of the children they were testing may be left behind because of lower intelligence compared to children who may just be lazy. The Simon-Binet exam used logical reasoning, finding rhyming words and naming objects as part of their IQ test.

Lewis Terman, an American psychologist revisited the the Simon-Binet exam creating a much more appropriate norm than the original tests so that the quotient could be measured with greater accuracy. The method to measure however only worked with children where the analysis was still based on multiplication of standard figures to find a result.

It was some 30 years later that “David Wechsler solved the problem of calculating adult IQ by simply comparing performance to the distribution of test scores, which is a normal distribution.” His method of analysis and discovering a better way to score these tests have helped create the more modern iterations of the IQ test used across the world.

## What are IQ tests used for?

IQ tests can be used for a variety of different purposes. These include:

- Schools

To help identify children who may be gifted and thus to be given extra support to achieve or equally, analyzing where children may require additional help in education.

- Military

When originally coined, the IQ tests were separated into ALPHA and BETA. The first is for new recruits, the second for those who pass training. It helped to identify those with candidates with intellectual deficiencies, psychopathic tendencies, nervous intangibility, and inadequate self-control.

- Recruitment professionals

The IQ test helps point out candidates who exhibit critical thinking skills, learning ability and problem solving.

- Individuals

This could just be for fun for many people, a bragging rights measure at the pub quiz or it could be done for genuine interest.

- Mensa

Mensa tries to identify those of a higher intellect in order to foster human intelligence for the benefit of humanity.

## Types of IQ tests

There are many different types of IQ tests with over 200 being last identified in a 2017 study. They are all trying to do the same thing but with different focuses on cognitive abilities and differentiate measuring tools.

Here is a selection of the different types of IQ tests currently being used:

- Cognitive Abilities Test (CogAT)

- Differential Ability Scales (DAS)

- Differential Ability Scales - Second Edition (DAS-II)

- Naglieri Nonverbal Ability Test (NNAT)

- Naglieri Nonverbal Ability Test 2 & 3 (NNAT2/NNAT3)

- Otis Lennon School Abilities Test (OLSAT)

- Otis-Gamma Test

- Stanford Binet

- Stanford Binet 5

- Woodcock-Johnson Test of Cognitive Abilities

- ACT Composite

- GRE

- Henmon-Nelson

- LSAT**

- PSAT (taken in junior year)

- PSAT (taken in senior year)

- CEEB

- SAT

- California Test of Mental Maturity (CTMM)

- Cattell

- Differential Ability Scales (DAS)

- Reynolds Intellectual Assessment Scales

- Stanford Binet

- Stanford Binet 5

However the two most commonly found and used IQ tests around the world are:

- The Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS)

- Raven's Progressive Matrices

## Are IQ tests accurate?

People often ask if IQ tests are accurate. There appears to be a variety of opinions on this subject. One of the common concepts around IQ test accuracy is that it depends on the tests that are being administered where scores can vary at different ages.

100,000 participants joined a recent study at the Canada Excellence Research Chair in Cognitive Neuroscience and Imaging to answer this question and completed 12 online cognitive tests that examined memory, reasoning, attention and planning abilities. They were also asked about their background and lifestyle. What they found was that a typical IQ study can’t determine general intelligence but that there are three different components that make up intelligence; short-term memory, reasoning and a verbal component.

However, as a general analysis, a professionally administered comprehensive test can still provide a general indication of someone’s mental abilities.

A better way to measure an individual's abilities to perform a task or to assess general intelligence is to opt for psychometric tests over IQ testing.

## Why psychometric assessments are a better choice for recruitment and development

We have learned that IQ tests are a way of measuring general intelligence based on a set of criteria, but psychometric testing (whilst still a form of testing intelligence) does more. Using a mixture of verbal and non verbal testing, this helps recruiters, managers and even CEO’s make better hiring and development decisions than a standard IQ test.

A psychometric test can be used to target better candidates for a role, give future insights into how the candidate can develop with the right training and even test with greater accuracy because everyone is treated equally.

The Thomas Aptitude test consists of five online tests that rely on processes such as thought, language, decision making, learning and memory. Each test measures a cognitive function:

- Perceptual Speed

- Reasoning

- Speed & Accuracy

- Spatial Visualization

- Word Meaning

Combined, these give an overall assessment of the candidate’s intelligence to perform for the role that they are being hired for.

Also known as the General Intelligence Assessment (GIA), it is designed to help businesses discover more about the candidate as well as providing detailed understanding that businesses can work with. The GIA can help you answer questions about your workforce including, ‘Can your people think on their feet?’, ‘Can they cope with the mental demands of the job?’, ‘Are they good problem solvers?’ and ‘How quickly can they learn?’.

## In summary

IQ testing has long been a standard bearer for those wanting to prove that they are “smarter than the average person.” Originally developed to analyze a child’s cognitive abilities, these tests have come on in recent years to identify potential future talent and discover “geniuses” among us.

Standardized tests are one way of analyzing an individual's intelligence. However, psychometric assessments such as Thomas' Aptitude assessment can analyze other aspects of an individual’s intelligence and more accurately predict someone's ability to perform a task in the workplace.

#
Time to Hire - A Complete Guide

8 minutes |

Updated
19 August 2024

By
Duncan Stimpson

Organizations go through phases of requiring new staff members and fulfilling new demand, that’s where ‘Time To Hire’ is introduced by many HR professionals. Time to Hire is one of the most important and frequently used metrics used by recruiters in understanding just how important the correct implementation of this process is can save organizations a lot of time and money.

In this guide we will take a closer look at what Time to Hire is, the Time to Hire Formula, why it is important and how to improve it.

As you will discover in our guide, recruitment metrics play a key role in the proper functioning of a business and its workforce management.

## What is time-to-hire?

Time to hire is a common and widely considered important recruiting metric. It measures the number of days between a candidate applying for a job and that same candidate accepting a job offer. The Time-to-hire metric is another way of analyzing how quickly a company can select and hire the best candidate.

From an operational perspective, it can give a clear figure to your HR team just how much time is needed to fill your open job position.

Time-To-Hire has become the metric that many understand in the recruitment world. They form part of the wider metrics which are used, such as:

- Time to fill

Measures the number of days it takes to fill an open position, from the date a job requisition is posted to the date a new hire accepts the position. This metric is often expressed as an average number of days when divided by the total number of hires or positions filled.

- Cost to fill

Which is a calculation that measures internal & external recruiting costs/number of hires.

- Interview to hire ratio

Interview to hire ratio is the number of candidates a hiring manager needs to interview to make an offer. An average interview to offer ratio is about 4.8:1. A good ratio is 3:1 or better.

As a key metric for human resource departments, time-to-hire refers to the amount of time that passes between when a job candidate is initially contacted by a company and when they accept the employment offer.

Time-to-hire is one of the key recruiting and hiring metrics. Time-to-hire shares the pedestal with cost-per-hire and quality-of-hire. These 3 metrics are the most important and most frequently used recruitment metrics.

##

## Time to hire formula

Time to Hire is calculated by using a simple formula which is: The day the candidate accepted the offer - The day the candidate entered the pipeline.

An example of this would be:

- Vacancy posted and promoted on the 1st day of the month

- An application is received on the 10th

- Between the 10th and 24th the candidate undergoes interviews, evaluations etc

- On the 25th - the candidate is provided with a job offer

- They accept the offer on the 28th

- The time between the date on which their application was received (10th) and the date on which they accepted the offer (28th) is the time to hire (18 days)

There has been some confusion in recent years about this calculation, but the example shown above will give the most accurate picture for the time to hire. Of course you can use a modified formula to calculate the average time to hire which is:

Time to hire (1) + Time to hire (2)... / Total number of job positions.

There is also some confusion that exists between the metrics ‘time to fill’ and ‘time to hire’; we will cover this later in the guide.

## Why is time to hire important?

So why is Time to Hire important? In essence, it gives you two key insights.

Recruiting efficiency which is the metric that measures the speed at which a candidate is processed, assessed, interviewed, and accepted for a job. The longer the time required indicates a slow and inefficient process with unnecessary bottlenecks.

Candidate experience is based on the metric of how long your candidate will choose to join your organization. Naturally, candidates would have a time to hire for two weeks rather than two months. A faster time to hire will lead to a better candidate experience.

Whilst these two insights alone give you great detail, mainly about the experience you are having and providing they also inadvertently offer more. The first is the indication of recruitment costs - as longer time to hire increases recruitment costs and raises the possibility of losing top candidates.

The second is just how much “candidate perception” of the organization is either positive or negative. Research has indicated that around 57% of job seekers lose interest if the recruitment process takes too long and this can reflect very negatively on the organization as a whole.

## Time to hire vs time to fill

As previously mentioned, there has been a lot of confusion in recent years regarding Time to Hire vs Time to Fill. Not only are they different, they can have an impact when used incorrectly.

They are both valuable metrics and HR departments can learn a lot from using these metrics. Time-to-hire refers to the total time it takes for a prospective candidate to apply until the second they accept a job offer, the Time-to-fill metric can be used to track the total amount of time company positions remain unfilled.

As discussed, they can both be essential metrics for an organization and they can be tracked and calculated differently to highlight efficiency processes.

Unlike the time-to-hire formula, the time-to-fill formula can vary depending on when the HR manager wants to begin measuring the time period. This could be from when a job opening is submitted for approval or when the job opening is actually approved, or when the job opening is first advertised. The end variable is the same as time-to-hire when a candidate accepts the job offer.

By using both metrics, you can develop a clearer understanding of what can be improved in the hiring process and in the different stages. Time to Hire will be focused on the time between a candidate applying and accepting an offer whilst Time to Fill can look at more of the internal metrics i.e. approval for a role posting.

## How to improve time to hire

We all want to have the best teams and every organization wants to have the best candidates apply. Time to Hire is important for the experience of candidates and ensuring top talent isn’t lost due to delays.

Another important reason to get Time to Hire done correctly is that it is an important exercise in saving costs - so what can be done to improve time to hire?

Here are just a few practical ways to shorten time-to-hire:

- Use efficiency improving recruitment tool

- Many of the very good tools on the market today will allow you to excel at the recruitment of staff by significantly contributing towards minimizing time to hire and maximizing the quality of candidate experiences.

- From email automation to letting the candidate know where they are in terms of the process, you can give a better representation of the organization and the recruitment process without having to do much other than set up a whole system.

- Assess all stages of the recruitment funnel

- Using the metrics identified previously, you can discover where the pinch points are in the recruitment process and make the necessary improvements to achieve a better outcome.

- Use both the Time to Hire and the Time to Fill calculations (as averages) to see where you can improve.

- Allocate realistic time periods to every stage of the process

- You need to be realistic with how long it can take to fill a position. You may have a very niche role or industry and the requirements of certain candidates may be completely different to more standard roles.

- An aspect of recruitment efficiency optimization can be to allocate appropriate periods of time to each stage which can then highlight where delays are occurring.

- This refers to the development of a structured hiring process.

- Improve your Employer Brand and careers page

- Candidates are likely to visit and review the company careers information multiple times during the hiring process.

- Employer branding describes an employer's reputation as a place to work and their employee value proposition.

- You want to be able to attract the best talent and one of the ways of doing this is by showing potential employees what the values and the culture of the organization are and how staff appear to feel about working there. Employer Brand, conveyed from this resource, alongside other information that keeps candidates on board.

- By improving the company careers page - fewer applicants will drop out or reject job offers.

- Present all of the information applicants typically seek - from the careers page into platforms which they will visit alongside your website.

- Use pre-employment candidate assessments and tests

- It takes time to administer cognitive ability assessments - the best solutions are efficient and effective.

- They enable the best, most suitable candidates to be identified quickly - and can contribute toward reducing time to hire.

## In summary

Recruitment metrics can help organizations get a firm understanding of where they can be better at recruiting top talent. The longer you may good people wait, the worse the outcome. Understanding Time-to-Hire is one of the best ways to get an idea of what you can do better as an organization to get your perfect candidate.

#
The Importance of Intelligence Tests in Modern Recruitment

6 minutes |

Updated
22 October 2024

By
Caitlin Meyer

Finding the right candidate in an ever-changing environment has become critical to business success.

Over the last few decades, businesses have utilized a variety of tools to get the people they think are suitable for the role; with varying degrees of results.

Whether it has been guesswork, a gut feel, standard IQ tests or even a mixture of all three, whatever the method, businesses have tried to find an answer to effective recruitment. This poses the question, what else is there and does it work?

We believe that there is an answer and it lies within intelligence tests. Over the course of this guide, we will look into the importance of intelligence tests in recruitment, how they work, and the overall advantages of doing these tests.

At Thomas our General Intelligence Test measures an individual's aptitude in 5 key areas: Reasoning, Perceptual Speed, Number Speed & Accuracy, Word Meaning and Spatial Visualization.

## What are intelligence tests for recruitment?

We describe intelligence tests as, “the skill required to test a candidate’s ability to perform specific tasks and react to a range of different situations.” Known also as aptitude assessments, or even perceptual speed or cognitive ability assessments, they help “give a detailed understanding of how quickly a person will adapt to a new role or regime.”

Understanding a candidate’s ability to perform tasks or knowing how they will react to different situations is of course a huge advantage. Let’s take a look at why that is and how it can benefit in the recruitment process. So, why are they good for managers?

It feels like a simple question therefore there must be a simple answer, right? Well kind of. In short, knowing if your new employee has the ability to carry out the work is of course an advantage. These kinds of assessments however do something further.

They are not standard IQ tests, they measure something else. Intelligence assessments are trying to uncover insights across different disciplines. As a business manager, if your line of work poses daily challenges, you want someone that can demonstrate the ability to adapt and change and show the attitude to do this before hiring.

Of course, there are other stakeholders that would benefit from this kind of testing as well; HR professionals and hiring managers for example. With workplaces becoming more virtual and globally disjointed, tasks changing based on new ways of working and thinking, being prepared and having staff that are prepared is always a key advantage.

If done correctly, internal recruitment using intelligence tests can help identify tomorrow’s leaders. ‘A business is only as good as the people that it employs’ as the old saying goes.

## How are intelligence tests performed?

Depending on who provides the test there will be variances across the board. Thomas’ General Intelligence Assessment (GIA) tests candidates through a mixture of verbal and non verbal testing.

Verbal tests such as verbal reasoning and situational judgment, assess an individual’s ability to analyze verbal data and make astute decisions. Non-verbal tests normally include numerical reasoning or inductive reasoning, assessing someone’s ability to handle numerical data, patterns and problem-solving.

Thomas’ GIA consists of five online tests that rely on processes such as thought, language, decision making, learning and memory. Each test measures a cognitive function, for example;

- Perceptual Speed

- Reasoning

- Speed & Accuracy

- Spatial Visualization

- Word Meaning

Combined, these give an overall assessment of the candidate’s intelligence to perform for the role that they are being hired for.

## What are the advantages of using intelligence tests in recruitment?

For many years, the IQ test has been a conversation starter as well as a recruitment assessment tool. Intelligence Quotient (IQ) was established in the early 1900s as a way to create a standardized measure of intelligence. This is great if you want to compare how smart you are to someone else in a bar discussion, but when it comes to the workplace, other key elements are required.

An intelligence test is designed to understand ability. It does this by assessing critical thinking, learning abilities and so on. Thomas’ General Intelligence Assessment (GIA) measures an individual's aptitude in 5 key areas: Reasoning, Perceptual Speed, Number Speed & Accuracy, Word Meaning and Spatial Visualization.

So how does it help recruiters? Here are five reasons how it can help.

### 1. It makes recruitment more targeted

If you have a specific role that you are looking to get fulfilled, already knowing if the candidate can learn or adapt to the new job or regime is a bonus from the get-go. It also removes from the selection those that aren’t suitable but may be for a different position.

### 2. It saves time and money

Before a candidate steps into the office, knowing if they have the skills to perform the tasks is a massive advantage. Our test is performed online and we get a body of data from the results that help identify the candidates you want to speak to saving time from having to meet and talk to everyone or a large group of candidates over the course of a few days.

### 3. You get future insights into your candidates

Not only will you be getting a more rounded selection of candidates based on what they are trying to achieve with a move into your business, you get an insight into how they can problem solve and perform moving forwards.

### 4. Your candidates are treated equally in testing

Some people struggle with interviews, others excel. This does not mean that the candidate who has great people skills might be right for the role or vise versa. What this does do is focus on the strengths and weaknesses that you won’t get from a standard sit-down interview; making this process fairer to the candidates and to the business involved.

### 5. Recruitment is adapting to an ever-changing working environment

With recent global events face-to-face meetings are harder and technology can’t always be trusted. In an ever-changing environment having more data to base decisions is going to be crucial and with online testing that helps you get the pick of the candidates you want.

Intelligence assessments have become a critical part of the recruitment process. They not only give valuable information and insights, they help determine and identify the candidates that can show the skills to help garner long term results. Used correctly, businesses can pick out individuals that show how much they can adapt, learn and grow within the business whilst also reducing costs and saving time.

Thomas’ GIA is designed to help businesses discover more about the candidate as well as providing detailed understanding that businesses can work with. The GIA can help you answer questions about your workforce including, ‘Can your people think on their feet?’, ‘Can they cope with the mental demands of the job?’, ‘Are they good problem solvers?’ and ‘How quickly can they learn?’.
