body:
#
What Is Emotional Intelligence and Why It Matters at Work

14 minutes |

Updated
09 July 2026

By
Duncan Stimpson

Emotional intelligence in the workplace is the ability to recognise, understand and manage emotions in a way that supports effective communication, sound judgement and stronger working relationships. For leaders and HR teams, it offers a practical lens for understanding how people respond under pressure, collaborate across functions and influence the performance of those around them.

In modern organizations, technical capability alone rarely determines success. Managers need to build trust, handle difficult conversations, adapt their approach to different people and make decisions with awareness of both business priorities and human impact. Emotional intelligence supports these outcomes by helping individuals regulate their own responses and interpret the emotions, motivations and behaviors of others more effectively.

This guide explains what emotional intelligence means at work, why it matters for leaders and teams, how it shows up in everyday workplace situations and how organizations can assess and develop emotional intelligence in the workplace.

## What is emotional intelligence (EQ)?

Emotional intelligence, often shortened to EQ, is the ability to recognise, understand, manage and use emotions effectively. In the workplace, this means being aware of your own emotional responses, reading the emotional context around you and adapting your behavior in a way that supports better judgement, communication and relationships.

For leaders, emotional intelligence is particularly important because emotion influences how people respond to pressure, feedback, uncertainty, conflict and change. A technically capable manager may understand the commercial objective. An emotionally intelligent manager is more likely to understand how to bring people with them, where resistance is coming from and how to create the conditions for better performance.

Emotional intelligence is commonly discussed through several models. The Mayer and Salovey Four Branch Model focuses on how people perceive, use, understand and manage emotions. Daniel Goleman’s widely recognised framework describes five components of emotional intelligence: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills.

In practical workplace terms, emotional intelligence can influence how someone:

- responds to difficult feedback

- manages stress before it affects others

- notices when a colleague is disengaged or under pressure

- adapts communication style for different people

- handles disagreement without escalating conflict

- builds trust across teams and functions

There is also a useful distinction between EI and EQ. Emotional intelligence refers to the broader set of emotional and social capabilities. EQ, or emotional quotient, is often used when discussing the measurement of those capabilities through an emotional intelligence assessment or test.

## The benefits of emotional intelligence in the workplace

Emotional intelligence in the workplace helps people communicate clearly, manage pressure, build trust and work through difficult situations with more control. For leaders and HR teams, its value is practical: it supports better management, stronger collaboration, more constructive conflict resolution and more consistent employee development.

### Stronger communication

Clear communication depends on more than information. Tone, timing, listening and emotional context all affect how a message is received.

Employees with stronger emotional intelligence skills are often better able to adapt their communication style to the person or situation in front of them. For managers, this is especially important when giving feedback, explaining change, managing performance or supporting employees through uncertainty.

Workplace emotional intelligence helps leaders notice when someone is disengaged, hesitant or frustrated, then adjust the conversation before misunderstanding turns into conflict.

### Better conflict management

Conflict is part of working life, particularly in organizations where people are under pressure or managing competing priorities. Emotional intelligence helps people recognise when a conversation is becoming defensive or unproductive, and respond with more control.

The CIPD highlights the importance of early, informal conflict resolution and the role managers play in preventing workplace issues from escalating. Emotional intelligence supports this by helping managers understand different perspectives, separate the issue from the individual and create space for constructive discussion.

### More effective leadership

Leaders need to understand how people respond to pressure, how trust is built and when a team needs clarity, support or challenge. Managers who regulate their own reactions, listen carefully and respond consistently are better placed to guide people through difficult periods.

This also supports psychological safety. McKinsey connects psychological safety with team effectiveness, learning, retention, decision-making and performance. Emotional intelligence can help leaders create the conditions where people are more willing to speak up, share concerns and challenge ideas constructively.

### Improved collaboration

Collaboration relies on trust, clarity and the ability to work through difference. Emotional intelligence helps employees recognise that people may approach communication, decisions and pressure in different ways.

This matters in cross-functional teams, where priorities can compete and assumptions can form quickly. Stronger emotional intelligence can help teams listen across areas of expertise, challenge ideas without damaging relationships and maintain trust when work becomes difficult.

### Greater self-awareness and emotional regulation

Self-awareness helps people understand their own triggers, habits and impact on others. Emotional regulation helps them respond with control rather than reacting impulsively.

In leadership roles, this can shape the tone of an entire team. A manager who stays calm under pressure, handles feedback well and communicates consistently makes it easier for others to do the same.

### Stronger engagement and development conversations

Emotional intelligence can also improve the quality of manager-employee relationships. Gallup’s Q12 meta-analysis reports that employee engagement is linked with outcomes such as productivity, profitability, retention, customer loyalty and wellbeing. Emotional intelligence is not the only driver of engagement, but it can influence many of the manager behaviors that support it.

## The five components of emotional intelligence (EQ)

Daniel Goleman’s emotional intelligence framework is often grouped into five components: self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. In the workplace, these components help explain how people understand themselves, manage their responses and build productive relationships with others.

### 1. Self-awareness

Self-awareness is the ability to recognise your own emotions, strengths, limitations and behavioral patterns. For leaders, this means understanding how their mood, communication style and decision-making habits affect the people around them. A self-aware manager may recognise that they become impatient under pressure, or that their direct style can be useful in a crisis but less effective in a coaching conversation.

### 2. Self-regulation

Self-regulation is the ability to manage emotional responses before they affect behavior. At work, this can show up in how someone handles criticism, conflict, setbacks or uncertainty. A leader with strong self-regulation can stay calm during difficult conversations, respond thoughtfully to challenge, and avoid passing pressure down to the wider team.

### 3. Motivation

Motivation refers to the internal drive to improve, achieve goals and continue making progress, even when work becomes difficult. In a workplace setting, this might look like resilience, ownership and a willingness to learn from feedback. For managers, motivation also affects how they influence others. Leaders who understand what drives their people are better able to support development and sustain performance.

### 4. Empathy

Empathy is the ability to understand and consider the emotions, needs and perspectives of others. This does not mean avoiding difficult decisions. It means making those decisions with awareness of their human impact. Empathy helps leaders notice when employees are under pressure, understand why resistance may be forming and adapt their communication without losing clarity.

### 5. Social skills

Social skills describe the ability to build relationships, communicate effectively and influence others constructively. In leadership roles, this includes giving feedback, resolving conflict, facilitating collaboration and creating trust across teams. Strong social skills help managers move conversations forward, especially when priorities compete or emotions are high.

### Five components at a glance

ComponentWhat it means at workWhy it matters

Self-awarenessUnderstanding your emotions, habits and impact.Helps leaders manage their behavior more intentionally.

Self-regulationResponding with control under pressure.Reduces impulsive reactions and supports better judgement.

MotivationStaying focused on improvement and progress.Supports resilience, ownership and performance.

EmpathyUnderstanding other people’s perspectives.Improves trust, communication and people management.

Social skillsBuilding productive working relationships.Supports collaboration, feedback and conflict resolution.

Together, these five components give leaders and HR teams a useful way to understand workplace emotional intelligence. They also provide a practical foundation for coaching, leadership development and employee development conversations.

## The difference between EQ and IQ

EQ and IQ measure different types of capability. IQ, or intelligence quotient, is associated with cognitive ability, reasoning and problem-solving. EQ, or emotional quotient, relates to how well someone recognises, understands and manages emotions in themselves and others.

In the workplace, cognitive ability may help someone analyse information, solve technical problems or make sense of complex data, whilst emotional intelligence helps them communicate that thinking clearly, respond well under pressure and work effectively with other people.

AreaIQEQ

Main focusCognitive ability and reasoning.Emotional and social capability.

Workplace relevanceProblem-solving, analysis and learning speed.Communication, self-management, empathy and collaboration.

Common use casesTechnical tasks, complex decision-making and role capability.Leadership, feedback, conflict resolution and team dynamics.

Development focusKnowledge, skills and cognitive performance.Self-awareness, emotional regulation and relationship management.

The key difference is that IQ focuses on how people process information, while EQ focuses on how people understand and manage emotional information.

For leaders and HR teams, the distinction is useful because performance rarely depends on one factor alone. A high-performing employee may need strong technical judgement, but they may also need the emotional intelligence skills to influence stakeholders, handle feedback, manage conflict and support others through change.

## Examples of emotional intelligence in the workplace

Emotional intelligence in the workplace is visible in everyday behavior. It shows up in how people listen, respond to pressure, give feedback, manage disagreement and adapt their communication style.

### Leadership conversations

A manager needs to speak with an employee whose performance has dropped. A low-EQ response might focus only on the missed targets. A more emotionally intelligent response would still address the performance issue, but would also explore context, listen carefully and agree clear next steps.

### Feedback

Emotionally intelligent feedback is direct, specific and constructive. It avoids personal criticism and focuses on behavior, impact and improvement. For example, instead of saying, “You are not communicating well,” a manager might say, “When project updates come late, other teams struggle to plan their work. Let’s agree a clearer update rhythm.”

### Conflict management

In a disagreement between colleagues, emotional intelligence helps people pause before reacting. Rather than assuming negative intent, they look for the underlying issue. That might involve clarifying priorities, checking whether workload is creating pressure or helping both people understand how their communication styles differ.

### Team collaboration

In cross-functional work, emotionally intelligent teams listen across areas of expertise. They challenge ideas without turning disagreement into personal tension. This is especially important when teams are working under time pressure. People with stronger emotional intelligence are more likely to notice when frustration is building and bring the conversation back to the shared objective.

### Customer-facing roles

Emotional intelligence also matters in customer-facing teams. Employees may need to stay calm when a customer is frustrated, understand what the customer is really concerned about and respond in a way that protects the relationship. This requires self-regulation, empathy and clear communication, particularly when the employee cannot immediately give the customer the answer they want.

### Common emotional intelligence examples at work

- A leader noticing when a team is under pressure and adjusting priorities

- A manager giving difficult feedback without damaging trust

- An employee listening fully before responding to challenge

- A colleague recognising their own frustration and pausing before speaking

- A team resolving disagreement by focusing on shared goals

- A customer-facing employee staying calm and constructive during a difficult conversation

## What does low emotional intelligence look like at work?

Low emotional intelligence at work often shows up as poor self-awareness, limited emotional control or difficulty understanding how behavior affects others. In leadership roles, it can quickly shape the team environment because employees often take cues from how managers communicate, respond to pressure and handle disagreement.

Common signs include:

- reacting defensively to feedback

- interrupting or dismissing other people’s views

- struggling to stay calm during conflict

- blaming others instead of exploring the issue

- missing signs that employees are disengaged or under pressure

- communicating in a way that feels unclear, blunt or inconsistent

- avoiding difficult conversations until problems escalate

For employees, low emotional intelligence can create tension in day-to-day collaboration. A colleague may dominate meetings, misread feedback, respond badly to challenge or struggle to adapt their communication style. Over time, these behaviors can reduce trust and make teamwork harder than it needs to be.

For leaders, the impact can be wider. A manager with low emotional intelligence may treat pressure as urgency for everyone else, give feedback in a way that damages confidence or fail to notice when conflict is building within the team. They may still be technically capable, but their interpersonal impact can limit performance.

Low emotional intelligence does not always look dramatic: sometimes it appears as silence, avoidance or lack of awareness. A leader who avoids emotional discomfort may delay performance conversations, ignore tension between team members or fail to acknowledge the human impact of change.

The important point for organizations is that emotional intelligence can be observed in workplace behavior. Once those patterns are visible, they can be discussed, assessed and developed through feedback, coaching and structured employee development.

## Emotional intelligence and leadership

Emotional intelligence is a core leadership capability because leaders influence both the direction of work and the emotional climate in which that work happens. The way a manager communicates, responds to pressure and handles difficult moments can directly affect trust, motivation and team performance.

For senior leaders and HR teams, emotional intelligence is especially relevant in four areas: coaching, trust building, employee engagement and change management.

### Coaching and feedback

Emotionally intelligent leaders are better equipped to give feedback that is clear, specific and useful. They can challenge performance without making the conversation feel personal, and they are more likely to adapt their approach based on the individual’s confidence, experience and development needs.

This matters because feedback should lead to action. If an employee leaves a conversation feeling confused, defensive or discouraged, the message may not translate into better performance.

### Trust and engagement

Trust is built through consistent behavior. Leaders who listen well, follow through on commitments and respond fairly under pressure create a more stable team environment.

Emotional intelligence also helps managers notice changes in engagement. They may spot when an employee is withdrawing, becoming frustrated or losing confidence, then respond before the issue becomes harder to address.

### Change management

During change, employees often look to leaders for clarity and reassurance. Emotionally intelligent leaders can acknowledge uncertainty without losing focus. They explain the business context, listen to concerns and help people understand what the change means for their role.

### Leadership takeaways

- Emotional intelligence helps leaders communicate with clarity and judgement.

- Stronger self-awareness improves consistency under pressure.

- Empathy supports better coaching, feedback and change conversations.

- Social skills help leaders build trust across teams and functions.

- Emotional intelligence data can support more targeted leadership development.

For organizations, emotional intelligence leadership is not about personality preference. It is about understanding the behaviors that help leaders build trust, manage pressure and get better outcomes from their teams.

## Emotional intelligence in hiring and talent decisions

Emotional intelligence can play an important role in hiring, promotion and talent planning, particularly for roles that rely heavily on communication, leadership, customer relationships or cross-functional collaboration.

Technical capability shows whether someone can perform the task. Emotional intelligence helps indicate how they may work with others while doing it. That distinction matters when organizations are hiring managers, developing future leaders or building teams that need to perform under pressure.

In recruitment, emotional intelligence can help employers understand how a candidate may:

- respond to challenge or feedback

- communicate with different stakeholders

- manage pressure in demanding situations

- build trust with colleagues or customers

- handle conflict constructively

- adapt their style to different working relationships

For leadership hiring, emotional intelligence is especially relevant. A candidate may have strong experience and technical knowledge, but still struggle to coach others, manage difficult conversations or build engagement across a team. Assessing emotional intelligence alongside other role requirements can give hiring teams a more rounded view of potential fit.

It can also support fairer and more consistent decision-making. Rather than relying only on interview impressions, organizations can use structured methods such as behavioral interviews, emotional intelligence assessments and wider talent assessment data to understand how someone is likely to behave at work.

## How organizations measure emotional intelligence

Organizations measure emotional intelligence to understand how people recognise emotions, manage responses, build relationships and operate under pressure. For HR and leadership teams, measurement helps move emotional intelligence from a broad concept into something that can be discussed, developed and applied more consistently.

There are several ways to assess emotional intelligence at work.

### Emotional intelligence assessments

Structured emotional intelligence assessments can help organizations understand how individuals perceive and manage emotions. These tools are often used in recruitment, leadership development, coaching and employee development planning.

A well-designed emotional intelligence assessment can provide insight into areas such as self-awareness, emotional regulation, empathy, motivation and relationship management.

### Behavioral interviews

Behavioral interviews can explore how someone has handled emotionally complex situations in the past. For example, a hiring manager might ask how a candidate responded to difficult feedback, managed conflict in a team or supported a colleague during a high-pressure period.

The value comes from asking consistent questions and assessing responses against clear criteria.

### 360-degree feedback

360-degree feedback can help leaders understand how their behavior is experienced by others. This is particularly useful because emotional intelligence is partly about impact. A manager may believe they communicate clearly, but peers or direct reports may experience their approach differently.

### Manager observation and development conversations

Managers can also identify emotional intelligence skills through day-to-day behavior. This might include how someone receives feedback, adapts their communication style, handles pressure or builds trust with colleagues.

### Main approaches to measuring emotional intelligence

- Emotional intelligence assessments

- Behavioual interview questions

- 360-degree feedback

- Manager observation

- Coaching and development conversations

- Wider talent assessment data

The strongest approach is usually a combined one. Assessment data can provide structure, while feedback and observation add workplace context. Together, they help organizations make more informed decisions about hiring, leadership development and employee growth.

## Emotional intelligence tests and assessments

Emotional intelligence tests and assessments help organizations understand how people perceive, understand and manage emotions at work. They can be useful in recruitment, leadership development, coaching and employee development, particularly when interpersonal judgement is important to role success.

Most emotional intelligence assessments fall into two broad categories.

### Self-report assessments

Self-report assessments ask individuals to rate their own emotional behaviors, preferences and perceptions. These can provide useful insight into how people see themselves, including their confidence, empathy, emotional regulation and relationship management.

The benefit of this approach is that it can reveal patterns that may not be obvious through performance data alone. The limitation is that responses depend on self-awareness and honesty, so results should be interpreted alongside other evidence.

### Ability-based assessments

Ability-based assessments ask people to respond to tasks or scenarios designed to measure how they identify, understand or manage emotions. These can help assess emotional reasoning, but they may not always show how someone behaves in their real workplace environment.

### Using assessment results responsibly

Emotional intelligence tests should not be treated as pass-or-fail tools. Their value comes from helping HR teams, managers and individuals understand likely strengths, development areas and workplace behaviors.

For example, assessment insight might support:

- leadership coaching

- team development

- recruitment conversations

- succession planning

- conflict resolution

- employee development plans

The most useful approach is to combine emotional intelligence assessment data with structured interviews, manager feedback, performance evidence and development conversations. This gives organizations a fuller view of how someone may communicate, collaborate and lead in practice.

## Process for improving emotional intelligence in the workplace

Improving emotional intelligence in the workplace starts with awareness, then moves into deliberate practice. For organizations, the goal is not to change someone’s personality. It is to help people understand their emotional patterns, manage their responses and build more effective working relationships.

A practical development process might include the following steps.

### 1. Build self-awareness

Employees need to understand how they respond under pressure, how they communicate and how their behavior affects others. This can be supported through reflection, coaching, manager feedback or an emotional intelligence assessment.

### 2. Identify specific development areas

Emotional intelligence is broad, so development should be focused. One person may need to work on emotional regulation. Another may need to improve empathy, listening or conflict management.

Clear development priorities make progress easier to measure.

### 3. Practise emotional regulation

Emotional regulation helps people pause before reacting. In practice, this might mean taking time before responding to difficult feedback, preparing for challenging conversations or recognising when stress is starting to affect communication.

### 4. Improve listening and perspective-taking

Leaders and employees can build emotional intelligence by listening for context, not only content. This means paying attention to what someone is saying, what they may be feeling and what might be influencing their behavior.

### 5. Apply learning in real workplace situations

Training is useful, but emotional intelligence develops through application. Managers can support this by linking development goals to real situations, such as feedback conversations, team meetings, conflict resolution or coaching sessions.

### 6. Review progress regularly

Emotional intelligence development should be reviewed through feedback, coaching and practical examples. Managers can ask what has changed, what still feels difficult and where the employee has applied new behavior successfully.

### Practical action checklist

- Use assessment or feedback to identify emotional intelligence strengths and gaps

- Choose one or two development areas to focus on first

- Practise pausing before responding in high-pressure conversations

- Ask for feedback on communication style and impact

- Use coaching conversations to reflect on real workplace situations

- Review progress regularly through manager or peer feedback

- Connect development goals to leadership, collaboration or performance outcomes

For HR teams, the most effective approach is structured and continuous. Emotional intelligence improves when people receive clear insight, practise new behaviors and are supported by managers who can reinforce progress over time.

## Using emotional intelligence data for employee development

Emotional intelligence data can help organizations make employee development more specific, fair and actionable. Instead of relying only on manager opinion, HR teams can use structured insight to understand how people communicate, respond to pressure, build relationships and manage emotionally complex situations.

This is particularly useful for leadership pathways, coaching programmes and team effectiveness initiatives. For example, assessment insight may show that a future leader has strong motivation and resilience, but needs support with empathy or conflict management. That creates a clearer development plan than broad feedback such as “improve people skills”.

Emotional intelligence data can support:

- individual coaching plans

- leadership development programmes

- team communication workshops

- succession planning

- manager capability reviews

- employee development conversations

The value comes from turning insight into action. A development plan might include targeted coaching, feedback practice, mentoring or real workplace goals linked to meetings, conflict resolution or performance conversations.

For leaders, emotional intelligence data also helps make development conversations more objective. Rather than focusing on personality, managers can discuss observed behaviors, workplace impact and practical steps for improvement.

## Frequently Asked Questions About Emotional Intelligence

### What is emotional intelligence?

Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognise, understand and manage emotions in yourself and others. At work, it helps people communicate effectively, handle pressure, resolve conflict and build stronger relationships.

### Why is emotional intelligence important at work?

Emotional intelligence is important at work because it influences how people collaborate, lead, give feedback and respond to difficult situations. For leaders, it can support better judgement, stronger trust and more effective people management.

### What are the five components of emotional intelligence?

The five commonly used components are self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skills. Together, they describe how people understand themselves, manage their responses and build productive relationships with others.

### How can emotional intelligence be improved?

Emotional intelligence can be improved through feedback, reflection, coaching and deliberate practice. Common development areas include listening, emotional regulation, empathy, conflict management and adapting communication style.

### How do organizations assess emotional intelligence?

Organizations assess emotional intelligence through structured assessments, behavioral interviews, 360-degree feedback, manager observation and coaching conversations. The strongest approach combines assessment data with real workplace context.

### What is the difference between EQ and IQ?

EQ relates to emotional and social capability, while IQ relates to cognitive ability and reasoning. In the workplace, IQ may support technical problem-solving, while EQ supports communication, collaboration, leadership and relationship management.

### What are examples of emotional intelligence in the workplace?

Examples include staying calm during conflict, listening before responding, giving constructive feedback, adapting communication style, noticing when a colleague is under pressure and managing difficult conversations with professionalism.

### What are examples of emotional intelligence in the workplace?

Examples include staying calm during conflict, listening before responding, giving constructive feedback, adapting communication style, noticing when a colleague is under pressure and managing difficult conversations with professionalism.

## Conclusion

Emotional intelligence in the workplace gives leaders and HR teams a practical way to understand how people communicate, respond to pressure, manage relationships and contribute to team performance. It supports better leadership, stronger collaboration, more constructive conflict resolution and more targeted employee development.

For organizations, the next step is to make emotional intelligence visible and actionable. That means looking at how it shows up in everyday behavior, using structured assessment where appropriate and supporting people with coaching, feedback and development plans.

When leaders understand emotional intelligence more clearly, they can make better people decisions and build teams that work together with greater trust, clarity and resilience.

body:
#
Neuroticism Personality Trait

7 minutes |

Updated
21 August 2024

By
Caitlin Meyer

Social psychologists have spent years studying personality and the human condition, in this they discovered the Big 5 personality traits of which, Neuroticism is just one. Using the acronym, OCEAN, the big five include, Openness, Conscientiousness, Extroversion, Agreeableness, and of course, Neuroticism.

As with all personality traits, individuals work on a scale of high to low and it’s no different with neurotic personalities. In its most simplest form, neuroticism means we have a negative response to frustration, perceived loss, or feeling threatened.

In today’s guide we are going to take a closer look at neuroticism, understand how it impacts behavior in the workplace and why it’s important to consider neurotic tendencies in the hiring process. Finally we will discuss how the Thomas workplace personality test can help you measure and understand neuroticism.

## What is neuroticism?

It is arguably one of the most debated personality traits where some see it as a compliment and others not so much. A simple way to think of neuroticism is how well an individual can manage stress and experience negative emotions in relation to these circumstances. Another way to understand neurotic behavior is to consider it as “emotional stability”.

We have all encountered a neurotic personality and reading some of the descriptions across the internet and in this guide, you may have experienced these emotions and thoughts yourself over the course of your lifetime.

Neuroticism, like all other personality traits, lives on a sliding scale of high to low and it isn’t uncommon to encounter these emotions and feelings in the course of your life. When you hear that someone is neurotic, there can be a negative attitude applied to this description but when you analyze neuroticism more closely, it does have advantages.

Being able to understand that neuroticism is our response to stressful situations opens up the definition a little more. We will all experience stress in our lives, how we deal with it is the way to better understand our emotional stability.

Like with other personality traits, neuroticism can impact our behavior in the workplace and even the working environment. We will discuss this a little further on, but there are benefits associated with being neurotic in the workplace. From ruminating on decisions - which require more in depth thinking to greater emotional depth - which helps with empathy and understanding other people’s struggles.

##

## What it means to be neurotic

What does it mean when someone is called neurotic? As previously mentioned, there are negative connotations to this however, it is another way of defining emotional stability. How well someone deals with stress is the core matter of neuroticism.

In doing so, social psychologists have tried to separate anxiety and neuroticism in definitions over the years. Understanding whether you have anxiety or if you suffer from neuroticism is a key starting point. Neurotic behavior can be mis-interpreted as anxiety and vice versa. At its core, anxiety is about how we deal with stressful situations leading to the “fight or flight” response which can be acute and disrupt our day to day thinking in severe cases.

Fundamentally, understanding if you are neurotic or suffering with anxiety is all dependent on how the anxiousness manifests. Is it frequent, often happening throughout the day or in more stressful situations? Does it ever get really bad - worse than it should be by a significant margin? Is it very hard to control? Understanding your response identifies if this is more anxiety or neurotic behavior.

Signs of neuroticism include:

- Social anxiety

- Tendency to feel stressed

- Emotional instability

- Resort to coping mechanisms (eating, alcohol etc.)

- Personal insecurities

- Can be pessimistic about circumstances

- Volatile with their emotions

- On the constant look out for dangerous situations

- Experiences discomfort with change

- Can easily feel stressed and tense

- Can appear withdrawn when suffering with anxiety

- Ruminates and fantasizes

- Rarely ever feels satisfied with life

- Suffer from feelings of guilt

- Weakened immune system, often having colds and flu

## How neuroticism impacts behavior in the workplace

Naturally, with all other personality traits, neuroticism can impact behavior in the workplace. If you were to consider - as you should - neuroticism on a scale, you need to understand that this behavior can impact people differently and thus impact the workplace in a different manner as well.

### Disadvantages of neuroticism

Neuroticism can influence people at work in different ways. For example:

- Lower ability to focus over extended periods

This can be from being easily distracted to letting their emotions take over during the day and focusing on those inputs.

- Indecision

Neurotic personalities can struggle to make decisions, ruminating for long periods of time.

- Uncertainty

Part of neuroticism is the way that you perceive change and uncertainty. More neurotic people suffer with uncertainty and changes.

- Anxiety

As discussed, neuroticism holds many of the same traits of anxiety. Better understood as “fight or flight” conditioning, anxiety can affect people in many different ways.

### Advantages of neuroticism

Whilst neuroticism has been represented negatively, it does also have many upsides which are usually forgotten about. These include:

- Thoughtfulness, reflection and rumination

Can be valuable in many roles. Particularly useful in roles which require more reflection and in anticipating and mitigating problems.

- Constant awareness of pitfalls

Beneficial in a wide range of roles. That insight and consideration in mitigating problems is useful at team leadership levels as well as in project management roles.

- Realistic self-awareness

A more honest self-appraisal can be a refreshing change for many organizations. It removes boastful attitudes to work and other colleagues which can disrupt.

- Emotional depth

This can help support team cohesion which helps with empathetic tendencies and understanding other people’s struggles.

There are roles which would suit people with neurotic tendencies which include: entrepreneurs, academics, artists, freelancers, florists, accountants and even yoga instructors.

When it comes down to understanding neurotic tendencies, consider how roles that match the more positive traits of this personality can be of use within your organization. Think of roles which require more evaluation, attention to detail and of course, in-depth thinking. Managed correctly, these roles can influence positive change with the business and in roles.

##

## Why neuroticism is important in hiring decisions

Understanding the big 5 personality traits is important for any employer and recruiter. Giving insights into how someone will behave under certain circumstances or how they can progress within the company is of considerable importance. What employers are trying to understand is the individual’s suitability for a role and studying personality traits is one of the key ways of doing so.

Alongside the other personality traits of Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion and Agreeableness, Neuroticism plays its part in creating the analysis for employers to use in their hiring decisions.

It’s not all negative, a little neuroticism can be good for the soul. “These personality types tend to be intelligent, humorous, have more realistic (if cynical) expectations, a greater self-awareness, drive and conscientiousness, they take fewer risks, and have a strong need to provide for others,” says psychiatrist Grant H. Brenner M.D., FAPA, co-founder of Neighborhood Psychiatry, in Manhattan.

Alongside this, neurotics have more experience handling negative emotions which can help facilitate empathy and an understanding of other people’s emotions and behavior.

When you bring together the many upsides of neurotic behavior - and the downsides - it’s useful for employers to understand if they have a candidate who can deal with stressful environments and how they work interpersonally with other employees before making that decision.

## How Thomas assessments measure workplace personality

The Thomas workplace personality assessment can be used to understand a candidate or employees level of neuroticism, and wider personality.

Using the globally recognized and respected big 5 psychological theory the High Potential Trait Indicator (HPTI) as we also call it, can also help to identify leadership potential.

The big five personality traits cover Openness, Conscientiousness, Extroversion, Agreeableness, and Neuroticism and present results in an easy to understand format that can give insight into a candidate’s suitability for a role.

Developed by Ian MacRae and Adrian Furnham in 2006, the HPTI has been designed based on an ‘optimality’ model, which assumes that personality traits can be considered ‘optimal’ based on the requirements of a particular job role or position, such as senior executive leadership.

Whether you are looking for the next superstar to join your team, possibly even start to change team dynamics or you want to measure the level of neuroticism in your workplace, the HPTI assessment can analyse all the data in one place giving you insight in minutes.

## In summary

Neuroticism is how well an individual can manage stress and experience negative emotions in relation to these circumstances. Another way to understand neurotic behavior is to consider it as “emotional stability”.

Whilst it is usually associated with negative interpretations, neuroticism does have many benefits and can be useful for employers to consider some of these upsides when hiring in their teams. From in-depth thinking to empathy, neurotic behavior can also be good for the office environment.

Managed correctly, considering those who test higher in neurotic tendencies can be considered a good hire in the office environment.

# Candidates

# Thomas Assessment Guides for Candidates

Whether you are taking a Thomas assessment as part of a recruitment process or for your own personal or professional development, we want to help you feel prepared.

## Completing a Thomas assessment

By having a good understanding of the assessment and what to expect, you are more likely to perform at your best and have more confidence when completing other assessments in future. As you prepare to complete your psychometric assessment, remember this is an opportunity to gain valuable insights into your strengths, preferences, and potential areas for growth.

##

Thomas' Behavior assessment

The Thomas Behavior assessment, also known as the Personal Profile Analysis (PPA), evaluates how a person prefers to behave and communicate in the workplace.

### Background & Theory

Dr. Thomas Hendrickson adapted William Moulton Marston’s DISC theory to create the Thomas Behavior assessment (PPA) in 1958, designed specifically for workplace settings. Marston's theory of human behavior (1928, 1931) proposes that our behavior is shaped by how comfortable we feel in different situations and how motivated we are to influence those situations. This framework identifies four key behavioral factors: Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, and Compliance. These factors form a matrix that reveals a person's typical interaction patterns. The assessment highlights personal behavioral preferences—there is no "ideal" style, as individuals naturally favor certain approaches over others.

### Assessment Instructions

- There is no "correct" behavioral style. The assessment measures your natural preferences, so you cannot pass or fail.

- Your first response is usually the most accurate. Be spontaneous and truthful when answering.

- Completing the assessment without interruptions helps you focus. Although it is not timed, the assessment typically takes about 8 minutes.

- Base your answers on how you behave in your current job or most recent professional role. If you don’t have professional experience, answer based on your behavior at home.

Throughout the assessment, you will be presented with sets of four words. For each set, choose the word or phrase that most describes how you operate in your current job and the one that least describes you.

Some questions may be challenging to answer if all or none of the words resonate with you. These questions help capture the subtleties of your behavior, so it’s important to select the words that best reflect you.

##

Thomas' Aptitude assessment

The Thomas Aptitude assessment measures an individual's ability to quickly learn, process, and retain new skills and information.

### Background & Theory

Developed by Dr. Peter Dann in 2022, this assessment has repeatedly been grounded in research, reviewed by the American Psychological Association in 1998, and more recently in a meta-analysis by Sackett et al (2022). The findings showed that higher cognitive ability, or aptitude, as measured by the Thomas Aptitude assessment, is directly linked to improved employee productivity and performance. This tool provides an objective evaluation of a person’s capabilities, regardless of their qualifications or experience.

### Assessment Instructions

- The assessment is timed, so completing it as quickly and accurately as possible is important.

- Complete the assessment in a quiet, distraction-free environment.

- The assessment consists of 5 sub-tests, each lasting between 2 to 5 minutes.

- Including instructions and practice examples, the assessment takes 30-45 minutes to complete.

- For best results, complete the assessment in one sitting.

- We strongly recommend reading the Aptitude Example Booklet below for more information on the types of questions you'll encounter.

- If you are aware of any factors that could affect your ability to complete the assessment, please inform the person who asked you to take it.

Aptitude Example Booklet

### Technical Requirements

Before starting the assessment, you will need to set up your:

- Device: Use a desktop computer or laptop (PC or Mac) as the assessment will not run on mobile devices such as tablets or smartphones.

- Browser: Ensure you're using the latest version of your chosen web browser (Mozilla Firefox, Microsoft Edge, Google Chrome, or Safari). The assessment does not support Internet Explorer 11 or earlier versions.

- Background programs: Close any programs running in the background. Make sure pop-up windows and JavaScript are enabled.

- Network environment: It’s best to avoid completing the assessment at work, as some security settings may interfere with or block the assessment. We recommend using your home PC or Mac.

- Internet connectivity: The assessment will not be disrupted by internet connection issues, as all parts are loaded before it begins. No additional downloads occur during the assessment.

If the assessment is not functioning properly, try the following steps:

- Switch to a different web browser.

- Try using another computer.

If you continue to experience issues, consider these additional troubleshooting tips:

- For Google Chrome or Mozilla Firefox users: Turn on Chrome’s Incognito mode or Firefox’s Private Window to prevent browser extensions from interfering with the assessment.

- Temporarily disable any ad-blocking extensions.

##

Thomas' Personality assessment

The Thomas Personality assessment, also known as the High Potential Trait Indicator (HPTI), examines an individual’s personality traits and offers insights into how they work and interact with others.

### Background & Theory

Developed by Ian MacRae and Adrian Furnham at University College London (UCL) and High Potential Psychology Ltd in 2016, the HPTI is based on a trait model of personality. This model places individuals along a continuum of stable personality factors. Different points on this continuum indicate the presence or absence of thoughts and behaviors that define each trait. Certain levels of these traits can suggest a high potential for success or, conversely, the risk of traits that might derail success. Drawing from contemporary personality psychology, including the Big Five Model, the assessment focuses on traits most predictive of workplace performance. Research demonstrates that different personality trait levels are linked to success in various roles, making it a valuable tool for measuring workplace personality.

### Assessment Instructions

- There are no right or wrong answers, and you cannot pass or fail the assessment.

- The assessment is untimed; however, it typically takes around 8-10 minutes to complete.

- Try not to overthink the meaning of each statement. Be spontaneous and honest in your responses.

- Completing the assessment in a quiet, interruption-free environment helps with focus.

Throughout the assessment, you will be presented with 78 statements, and you’ll need to indicate how much you agree with each one on a scale from 1 (disagree completely) to 7 (agree completely).

##

Thomas Emotional Intelligence

Thomas’ Emotional Intelligence assessments evaluate an individual’s ability to understand and manage their own emotions and recognise and respond effectively to the emotions of others.

### Background & Theory

Grounded in established emotional intelligence research and theory, Thomas’ Emotional Intelligence assessments explore emotional intelligence as a measurable set of traits linked to how people understand themselves and relate to others. They provide a comprehensive view of the emotional factors that influence behaviour, communication, and relationships, offering valuable insight into how individuals prefer to work, interact, and perform in professional settings.

### Assessment Instructions

- There are no right or wrong answers, and you cannot pass or fail the assessments.

- The assessments are untimed.

- It is recommended to complete the assessment in a quiet, distraction-free environment to help you stay focused.

- Read each question carefully to ensure full understanding, but do not spend too long thinking about your response, as your first instinct is often the most accurate.

Complete the assessment in your preferred language. If that option is not available, select the next most suitable language.

### Structure of the assessments:

The assessments include a series of statements. For each statement, you will select a response on a scale from 1 (completely disagree) to 7 (completely agree).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### <h6 id>What are psychometric assessments?</h6 id>

Psychometric assessments are measures developed from validated psychological theories explaining specific elements of human functioning. They objectively and scientifically measure specific aspects of a person, and are often used to challenge subjective feelings, opinions, and biases. Such assessments provide in-depth, objective insights into the underlying aspects of a person, such as behavioural preferences, personality traits, and abilities. At Thomas, our assessments are based on strong, highly validated psychological science and over 45 years of academic and applied research.

### <h6 id>What are psychometric assessments used for?</h6 id>

Psychometric assessments can be used across business, education and sport settings to address an array of people decisions. Commonly, they are used to recruit new individuals, identify individuals with the potential to be developed in specific areas, to increase team cohesion, provide career advice, coach individuals in attaining personal or professional goals, and to optimise organisational structure.

### <h6 id>What makes a good psychometric assessment?</h6 id>

Good psychometric assessments are valid, reliable and fair. A valid assessment can be shown to measure what it says it does, and to be related to workplace outcomes such as performance or engagement. A reliable assessment can be shown to be accurate, i.e., if you completed it twice you would get very similar results. A fair assessment can be shown not to adversely impact any group of people. Thomas assessments are independently audited by the British Psychological Society (amongst other international bodies) to ensure we meet their strict criteria.

### <h6 id>What influence do the assessment results have on hiring decisions?</h6 id>

Assessments are designed to be used in conjunction with other elements of the recruitment process, such as interviews, references, work simulation activities, etc. They objectively and scientifically measure specific aspects of a person and are often used to challenge subjective feelings, opinions, and biases. However, assessments are just one piece of the puzzle when getting to understand a person.

#
What is a Skills Gap Analysis & How to Conduct One

8 minutes |

Updated
19 August 2024

By
Duncan Stimpson

How do you know if the people working in your organisation have the skills to meet the daily demands of the modern business world? How do you measure if someone can develop or has the skills to develop? With over 300 million people set to be changing jobs and even career paths in the next decade, these are the questions that need to be asked by industries and organisations alike.

A skills gap analysis is the best way to ask that question, and understanding what is needed by your workforce and planning ahead for seismic changes in your industry is the best place to start.

From developing your workforce to creating individual learning and development, promoting strategic workforce planning and improving recruitment efforts, a skills gap analysis creates a competitive advantage for your organisation.

In this guide we are going to investigate the ideas behind a skills gap analysis, why they are important, how to conduct one - from identifying skills to measuring existing ones and give you an overall better understanding of this highly strategic tool that is used by organisations in every industry around the world.

## What is a skills gap analysis?

A skills gap analysis is understanding what the gap between the set of talent required for a job and the set of skills that a person actually possesses. A skills gap analysis is understanding what your organisation needs from a skill based level in order to strategically execute their plans for the future.

For employers, a skills gap analysis is to help provide a greater understanding of where there is a skills shortfall in order to achieve the defined goals of the organisation.

For employees a skills gap analysis means developing an understanding of what specific knowledge and skills are currently lacking in order to carry out their job to the best of their abilities.

The resulting outcome from this kind of gap analysis is that an organisation can identify where there are gaps in the current workforce and either recruit new employees to fill some of the more urgent requirements and skill levels or, invest in their current employees to upgrade their skills and capabilities.

Because skills gaps develop and evolve over time - or in some cases become more apparent over a longer period, there is a constant need to repeat a skills gap analysis - especially for organisations where strategic development of the workforce is required to stay ahead of the game.

## Why is skills gap analysis important

Being able to understand where you are lacking skills in your current organisation is of course a benefit but that’s not all. There are other benefits which must be considered including:

- Aiding the recruitment process

You know what you require, and what is going to be important to recruit for in the coming future.

- Enhances capabilities of existing employees

You develop your existing employees, reducing the need to recruit and costs saved in that area.

- Ensures an organisation has the skills / knowledge resources necessary to achieve goals

You are future proofing your ability to understand the market and deliver a product/service that matches your future goals.

- It creates a competitive advantage

If you can understand what skills are required to the changing marketplace, and then develop a team that can deliver in that field, you are creating the necessary advantages over your competitors in order to succeed.

## How to conduct a skills gap analysis

Firstly, you need to understand that a skills gap analysis is not something that is either done once and left alone or done every 10 years. It needs to be a constant process that is repeated whenever the objectives of the business are developed or changed.

You may need to perform a skills gap analysis when:

- Business objectives not being achieved

- Newly defined business objectives or goals

- Staff changes (people leaving)

- There is a change in market practices

- New legislation is implemented

- When new technologies are introduced

The skills gap analysis can fundamentally be broken down into three phases.

### 1. Identify skills requirements

The process starts by identifying what skills are actually required. What do you really need in order to execute your business strategy for the present and future. These need to then match what your business needs, goals and objectives are.

Top tip; list out your business objectives and map competencies to each of the objectives.

Secondly, you want to understand what technological developments for which skills and knowledge are likely to be required. For example, if you worked in business security in the early 2000s, it would have been likely unnecessary to know anything about cybersecurity but now, it is a fundamental skill that is required to do the job today.

Finally, you need to define what level of skill is required in order to carry out the job required - as identified. Do you need accreditations or would an online course of several hours be sufficient?

### 2. Measure existing skills

In order to successfully complete a skills gap analysis, you want to be able to understand what level of existing skills are present in your workforce. There are several tools that can give you a lot of information in this area including:

One to one performance reviews

Sitting down with managers and HR to understand where the base level of skill is per job is a good starting point. Someone may not realise that they’ve acquired new skills as well - this can be pointed out and developed in a training plan.

Skills assessments

Skills assessments can take many different forms but in essence they ​​identify the skills you have in relation to the job that is either being filled or has been filled and you are trying to understand what skills gaps there may be.

The most commonly used talent assessment tests:

- Skill assessment tests

- Psychometric tests

- Personality tests

- General mental ability assessments

- Integrity assessments

- Job knowledge tests

- Situational judgment tests

Behavioural assessments

Behavioural assessments help organisations and recruiting managers understand the level of interpersonal skills that a person has and help predict how they might respond to new & different scenarios.

Behavioural assessments help us to understand and explain what is happening to a person, why it is happening and help to predict when a behaviour might happen again.

360 feedback

The 360 feedback system is a process where employees are engaged to provide anonymous feedback on an individual in a business and give them rounded evaluations as to strengths and weaknesses and what can be further improved over a period of time following a development plan.

A series of different information points are presented in a report that is used to help the manager go through with the employee and create a tailored plan to get key skills, strengths and weaknesses aligned with the organisation and what can be improved moving forwards.

### 3. Fill identified skills gaps

Once the skill shortages have been identified, you need to fill the identified gaps. The information that has been collected can be used to help provide valuable insights into the current skills of the workforce and then equally, provide the right point of focus for your recruitment strategies.

I.e. you need more staff with SAP skills. You target your recruitment drive in areas where SAP is regularly recruited - be it on a temporary or permanent basis.

This developed insight also helps to support the need to develop skills within your current workforce. One major advantage of developing your team is that you save on recruitment costs whilst also showing the value that they have in your organisation. This will help with retention rates and provide a good opportunity for them and the organisation alike to grow focused on the same goals.

Developing your own team can take three main forms:

- Training

This could be done internally by someone who has a much deeper understanding of the subject and can create a learning environment for your team members who need upskilling to thrive or, if you had the budget to succeed, you may be able to hire a team to come in from the outside and train your teams. For example, many sales-based organisations will have regular training sessions with third party trainers and seasoned experts who teach this type of content for a living.

- Mentoring/coaching

As with training, mentoring and coaching can be a powerful tool and can be more targeted to smaller groups or individuals who need to upskill quickly. With many businesses having more seasoned staff in roles around the organisation, this could take a little more time to implement but it also helps provide a way to constantly motivate staff members and tap into knowledge of other team members at the same time.

- Outsourcing/contracting

Sometimes, your business needs to move faster and training is a solution that takes longer to implement. That's where outsourcing/contracting comes into play. Think of that example above about an SAP engineer - it could be for a short term contract and someone with experience in this field is easier to recruit for on a short term basis than having to train up staff - especially if the training costs too much or you won’t require that skill in the business strategy moving forwards.

## In summary

A skills gap analysis is understanding what your organisation needs from a skill based level in order to strategically execute their plans for the future. From developing your workforce to creating individual learning and development, promoting strategic workforce planning and improving recruitment efforts, a skills gap analysis creates a competitive advantage for your organisation.

The Thomas talent assessment platform can help you with a plethora of development needs including identifying and nurturing future leaders, improving employee engagement, leading through change and managing conflict effectively to keep people development at the heart of your business success.
