#
Leadership Assessments: Identify and Develop Future Leaders

Updated
09 July 2026

By
Duncan Stimpson

When the time comes to hire or promote a leader, many businesses will simply look at an individual’s achievements and knowledge and make a decision based on that. The problem is – this approach often fails because it hasn’t considered whether or not that person has the right personality traits to succeed as a leader.

Astute businesses use leadership assessments to help make the right hiring and promoting decisions, and to direct resources towards developing those with true leadership potential. Read on to find out all about leadership assessment – what it is, what the different tests are and how our tools can help your business thrive.

## Understanding Leadership Assessments and Why They Matter

Leadership assessments are tools to help assess someone’s management skills, and in today’s business landscape, they’re a critical part of good talent management and leadership development.

Taking a number of different forms (which we’ll come onto shortly), they’re a way for businesses to understand who in their organisation has the skills and attributes necessary for leadership, enabling the right recruitment, promotion and training decisions and allowing personalised development plans that nurture and develop strong leaders. They also increase the self-awareness of the employees being assessed, helping them improve their own leadership.

Is your business is struggling to identify who in your team has leadership potential? Or are you having difficulty with succession planning and leadership pipeline development? Leadership assessments are a powerful tool to help you focus on the right people – namely those with the skills and personality to help take your business into the future. Crucially, they can also help you identify talent gaps and assess the effectiveness of those currently in leadership positions within your business.

### Leadership Assessment and Development Go Hand-in-Hand

Leadership assessments are an important development tool, as the insights you’ll gain from it help you to formulate much more personalised development plans for employees or even for yourself. It’s not just about who to promote into leadership roles, but about helping those with potential to excel. For example, with awareness of someone’s strengths and weaknesses, you’re in an informed position to be able to identify the right type of training for them to set their career path on a successful trajectory. The self-awareness that comes from leadership assessment will also further aid an employee’s development.

### Effective Leadership Skills

Effective leaders tend to have a number of traits in common. These might include, but certainly aren’t limited to, things like:

- Strong decision-making skills

- Emotional intelligence and empathy

- Ability to adapt and improvise

- Comfort with ambiguity

- Strategic thinking

- Assertiveness

- Effective communication

Our assessments track competitiveness, conscientiousness, ambiguity acceptance, adjustment, curiosity and risk approach – six traits that psychologists have proven are key leadership qualities. So what are the different types of leadership assessment tests that will help you identify these characteristics?

## Types of Leadership Assessments and How They Work

There are a number of different types of leadership assessments out there to help you spot these traits, and here at Thomas we offer a comprehensive suite of them that you can combine to give you an array of valuable insights. These work using online psychometric testing, interviews and 360 degree feedback, and include:

### DISC assessments

DISC assessments, short for Dominance, Influence/Inducement, Steadiness/Submission, and Compliance, provide a comprehensive understanding of individuals' behaviour and motivations in the workplace. By identifying where individuals fall within these categories, you can tailor your management approach and communication style to maximise productivity and job satisfaction. Understanding how employees respond to different situations and tasks can also help in building effective teams and resolving conflicts. Overall, DISC assessments are a valuable tool if you're looking to enhance employee engagement and performance.

### 360-degree feedback

360-degree feedback provides a comprehensive evaluation of an individual's skills and performance through feedback from various sources including managers, colleagues, team members, and customers. This process offers valuable insights into a potential leader's strengths, weaknesses, and areas for improvement, helping to paint a complete picture of their capabilities at work. By gathering constructive and anonymous feedback from multiple perspectives, you can ensure a more accurate assessment of an individual's competencies, ultimately aiding in their development and growth within the company.

### Personality tests

Personality tests are assessments that aim to evaluate individuals on various traits such as conscientiousness, adjustment, curiosity, risk approach, ambiguity acceptance, and competitiveness. Conscientiousness refers to how organised and responsible a person is, while adjustment measures emotional stability and resilience. Curiosity assesses how open someone is to new experiences and information, whereas risk approach examines their willingness to take risks. Ambiguity acceptance evaluates how comfortable a person is with uncertainty, and competitiveness assesses their drive to succeed and excel. These tests are often used in recruitment processes or personal development to gain insight into an individual's traits and tendencies.

### Behavioural assessments

Behavioural assessments provide valuable insight into how individuals perceive their own responses to various workplace situations. These assessments typically evaluate traits such as communication style, decision-making processes, team collaboration, and problem-solving skills. By exploring how individuals believe they react in certain scenarios, you can better understand their potential strengths and areas for development. This information could help you to tailor training programs, support personal growth, and create a more cohesive and effective team.

### Emotional intelligence tests

Emotional intelligence assessments provide individuals with an insight into their ability to recognise, comprehend, and regulate their own emotions, as well as the emotions of others - skills that are crucial for success in various aspects of life, particularly in the professional environment. Research has shown that a high level of emotional intelligence is closely linked to effective leadership, communication, teamwork, and problem-solving. By understanding their own emotional intelligence, individuals can develop strategies to improve their interpersonal skills and enhance their overall performance in the workplace.

Harnessing the power of people science, leadership assessments typically take the results of a variety of these different assessment methods to create a rounded view of someone’s leadership potential. You can then use these insights in leadership development and team building, helping your business enjoy the benefits of stronger leaders and teams.

### What is a 360° Leadership Assessment?

While standard performance reviews are usually approached as one-to-one appraisals between an employee and their manager, a 360 degree leadership assessment takes a much more rounded view by encompassing a range of other perspectives.

These perspectives might include anonymous feedback from peers, clients or customers and those both above and below the employee in seniority. This gives you a far deeper insight into how an employee is viewed within and outside your business, assessing their strengths and weaknesses as experienced by a wider range of people than just their manager.

### More Than a Leadership Style Quiz – Real Development Insights

It’s worth noting that a leadership assessment like ours is much more than a simple personality quiz. A scientific, data-driven assessment will be far more reliable and detailed than the generic tests you’ll find online.

## Features of the Best Leadership Assessment Tools, and How to Choose the Right One For Your Business

There are a number of different leadership assessment tools and platforms out there, so how do you know which one is going to be right for your business? Here are some of the features to look out for.

- Variety of tests: look out for assessments that utilise the results of a variety of tests – behaviour, aptitude, personality and emotional intelligence – so that you gain the most accurate insights.

- Scientifically backed: the robust science behind our industry-leading assessment is backed by the British Psychological Society (BPS), giving you the confidence that you can trust the results.

- Ease of use: the best platforms are user-friendly and intuitive for both employer and employee, generating clear, actionable insights you can immediately put to good use.

- Customisation: opt for a tool you can customise to the needs of your business.

- Heritage: a long-standing heritage is a definite trust signal, and at Thomas our insights have been trusted globally for over 45 years.

- Support and training: this will help you make the most of the platform and the insights it can generate. We invite you to spend a day with our experts to dig deep into your team’s insights and see how you can strengthen your leadership and team.

With the right leadership assessment platform, you can integrate powerful insights about your potential future leaders into your personalised training and coaching programmes, making it a crucial part of your leadership development or even succession planning.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Here are some of the questions we’re most often asked about leadership assessments.

### What are leadership assessments?

Leadership assessment is the process of using tools and tests to help assess someone’s qualities as a potential leader. It looks at their personality, attributes, experiences and skills, assessing whether they’re right for leadership and addressing areas to develop.

### What is the purpose of a leadership assessment?

Businesses use leadership assessments to identify employees with leadership skills, helping them make informed decisions on who to train and promote. It looks at someone’s future leadership potential, and how likely it is that they’ll thrive in a more high-pressure role. This is based on an assessment of their personality and traits, rather than focusing too much on previous achievements.

### How do you identify potential leaders?

Leadership assessments recognise that a potential leader’s personality is as important (if not more important) than what they know. It uses tools to assess someone’s personality and attributes, providing a science- and data-based approach to talent management. These tools are highly effective at identifying the traits that make good leaders, approaching it from a variety of angles including personality and behaviour tests, 360 degree feedback and DISC tests.

### What is the difference between leadership assessments and professional assessments?

While professional assessments provide a general overview of who’s best suited to what functions, and help you match talent to roles, leadership assessments specifically focuses on whether or not a person’s traits, motivations and skills make them good management material.

### Why should you assess your talent?

Before allocating training resources, promoting internally or hiring externally, assessing your talent gives you valuable insights into someone’s potential as a leader – and so helps you make the right decisions. Making assessment a key part of your talent management strategy avoids wasting resources and budget on recruiting or promoting the wrong person, and ensures that investment made in an employee will see a good return.

## Unlock Leadership Potential with Thomas

If your business is on the lookout for future leaders, take a look around our website to explore our leadership assessment solutions. You’ll find lots of in-depth advice and guidance in our resources section, and when you’re ready, get in touch with our experts or request a demo to see how our leadership assessments can help your team.

#
Task-Oriented vs People Oriented Leadership

5 minutes |

Updated
10 July 2026

By
William Beaumont-Oates

Organizations need good leaders to succeed. They ensure clarity of vision and motivate their teams, and every leader has their preferred way in which they manage their team to ensure the job gets done. These are called leadership orientations.

There are two recognized types of leadership orientation - task-oriented leadership and people-oriented leadership. To effectively manage and motivate teams, it’s important to understand these styles and how to use them.

## Understanding task-oriented leadership

Let’s start with task-oriented leadership. Leaders who lean into this style are focused on tasks, goals, and efficiency. They don’t always request input from their teams but use their knowledge of their skill sets to delegate accordingly and ensure projects are completed on time. These leaders emphasize organization, structure, and achieving specific outcomes. They communicate concisely and manage their time well - and expect the same from others.

This approach has its advantages. Task-oriented leaders work well to deadlines, autocratically divvying up tasks between their teams to make sure all elements of a project can be completed in time and that no one part of the workforce machinery is jamming up the next. They are highly productive, and ensure the lines of responsibility for each role are clear to those in and adjacent to them.

These sound like ideal qualities when it comes to the success of any given organization. However, this leadership orientation has its downsides. When a leader is too task-oriented, they risk overlooking the needs of their employees as people, leading to low morale and potential burnout.

## Understanding people-oriented leadership

People-oriented leaders look at their people first, and tasks second. They are motivated by the needs, development, and wellbeing of their team, and use their skills in empathy and communication to build strong relationships with all team members.

Leaders who are people-oriented play a key role in employee satisfaction and inspire loyalty. They spearhead collaborative teams who feel supported to propose new ideas and take risks.

However, as people-oriented leaders tend to focus on maintaining positive relationships, they can run into difficulty when it comes to discipline. If a manager’s leadership orientation is too people-focused, attention can be drawn away from tasks and too much leeway can be expected around deadlines. Employees led by people-oriented leaders may be happy, but they may also be less efficient.

## Balancing task and people orientation in leadership

Leaders can make use of a few different methods to assess their leadership style. Understanding personal strengths, preferences and blind spots helps leaders build consistent leadership capability and adapt their approach more effectively across different situations and teams.

This is why all leaders need to strike a balance. They need to understand the different types of leadership orientations and their signifiers to get a feel for what their natural inclination is. With this knowledge and awareness, they can seek to find a balance that allows them to help their team get work done without being dictatorial or losing track of tasks. Leaders should always adapt to fit the organizational context and their team’s needs, recognizing if their situation calls for a more people-oriented or task-oriented approach and adapting as the situation evolves. Developing this flexibility is a key part of consistent leadership capability.

The need to call upon different leadership orientations may change on a day-to-day basis. On days with tight deadlines or sudden challenges, a task-oriented approach can get everyone in order and ensure all tasks are outlined and completed. The same leader who applied this technique may then recognize that, following the announcement of a restructure, a people-oriented approach is required to maintain morale and reassure their team. Leaders who can flex and strike a balance see a higher level of performance from their team. Bill Gates is known for his ability to transform his leadership style as the situation requires, and he is arguably one of the most successful leaders in the world.

## Assessing your leadership style

Leaders can make use of a few different methods to assess their leadership style.

Self-assessment and self-development require little investment other than time. To self-assess, leaders should look back on recent projects and teams they’ve managed and review how they handled those situations. They can look out for signs of task-orientation or people-orientation in their current interactions.

Feedback from peers and team members is another useful way of uncovering leadership style. This approach removes any of the leader’s personal bias from the equation, instead highlighting how those who have experienced their leadership viewed them. 360-degree feedback, which collates contributions from superiors, subordinates, and colleagues outside of their team, is a particularly effective tool in this work.

To dig down into leadership orientation, people can complete psychometric assessments. These tests use people science to discover an individual’s traits, including their workplace personality, behavior, emotional intelligence, and general aptitude. Add this all up and you’ll have a clearer picture of a person’s leadership orientation.

## Leveraging Thomas’ expertise

Thomas, the expert in people science in the workplace and recruitment, can help your leaders identify their natural leadership orientation through psychometric assessments. We can then work with you to provide bespoke training and coaching to help leaders develop a more balanced approach, enhancing both task achievement and team engagement.

Speak to one of our team today to find out more about our platform and training.

## The impact of leadership orientation on organizational success

Let’s recap: task-oriented leaders are good delegators and decision-makers; they ensure everything is completed on time but can overlook their employees’ well-being in doing so. People-oriented leaders, on the other hand, naturally lean towards empathy and relationship building, but this can lead to problems disciplining their teams, leading to slipping deadlines.

As such, understanding leadership orientations and striking a balance is key. Leaders who can adapt their style, turning one way or the other as a situation calls for it without pushing too hard in one direction, have the best impact on their team’s engagement, productivity, and adaptability. For more insights into developing effective leaders, explore the Leadership Development Hub.

To ensure the leaders in your organization have the techniques and awareness to do this right, speak to one of Thomas’ team today. Our platform was designed to make better leaders.

Self-aware, balanced leaders are needed to navigate the complex modern workplace and motivate busy teams for success. Understanding and utilizing leadership orientation will help your leaders reach their full potential.

#
Behavioral Assessments: The Complete Guide for Hiring

Updated
09 July 2026

By
Duncan Stimpson

Behavioral assessments help hiring teams understand how candidates are likely to work, communicate, respond to pressure and collaborate with others. Used well, they add structure to hiring decisions that might otherwise rely too heavily on CVs, gut feel or inconsistent interview styles.

For HR and talent acquisition teams, the value is practical. Behavioral assessments can support more consistent candidate evaluation, highlight workplace strengths and risks, and give hiring managers clearer evidence to discuss during interviews. They are not a replacement for human judgement. But they can make that judgement better informed.

This guide explains what behavioral assessments are, what they measure, the different types available, and how to use behavioral assessments to improve hiring decisions.

## What Is a Behavioral Assessment?

A behavioral assessment is a structured way to understand how someone is likely to behave at work. It looks at patterns such as how a person communicates, makes decisions, responds to change, works with others and approaches tasks.

In hiring, behavioral assessments give employers insight that a CV cannot show on its own. A CV can tell you where someone has worked, what roles they have held and which technical skills they claim. An interview can explore motivation, experience and role fit. But both can be affected by subjectivity. One hiring manager may prioritise confidence. Another may favour technical detail. Another may be influenced by how similar a candidate feels to previous high performers.

That is where behavioral assessment tools can help. They give recruiters and hiring managers a more consistent way to assess workplace behavior against the needs of a role. However, behavioral assessments should not make the hiring decision alone. Instead, they add another layer of evidence, helping teams ask better interview questions, compare candidates more fairly and understand how someone may perform in a real working environment.

## What Do Behavioral Assessments Measure?

Behavioral assessments measure the work-related preferences and tendencies that influence how someone is likely to behave in a role. For hiring teams, this means looking beyond experience and technical capability to understand how a candidate may approach people, pressure, decisions and day-to-day responsibilities.

### What behavioral assessments typically measure:

- Communication style: How someone shares information, listens, persuades or adapts their message for different people.

- Workplace behavior: How they approach tasks, deadlines, structure, autonomy and accountability.

- Motivation: What may energise them at work, such as challenge, recognition, stability, collaboration or independence.

- Decision-making preferences: Whether they tend to move quickly, seek detail, involve others or rely on evidence before acting.

- Adaptability: How they may respond to change, ambiguity, setbacks or shifting priorities.

- Teamworking tendencies: How they collaborate, handle conflict, contribute to group goals and build working relationships.

- Leadership behaviors: How they may influence others, give direction, support development or manage pressure.

- Workplace strengths and risks: Where their natural style may support performance, and where it could create friction in certain environments.

For example, a candidate who prefers fast-paced decision-making may suit a commercial role where momentum matters. The same style could be harder to manage in a highly regulated role where detailed review is essential. Neither profile is automatically better. Context does the heavy lifting.

## Why Behavioral Assessments Matter in Hiring

Behavioral assessments matter in hiring because they help teams make decisions using structured, role-relevant insight rather than relying on interviews alone. Instead of asking, “Did we like this person?”, hiring managers can ask sharper questions:

- Does this candidate’s behavioral style match the demands of the role?

- Where might they perform strongly?

- Where could they need support?

- How should we explore potential risks during interview?

- How might they work with the existing team?

Behavioral hiring assessments can also support fairer candidate evaluation when used responsibly. They give every candidate the same structured assessment experience and help reduce over-reliance on subjective impressions. A confident interviewee is not always the best performer. A quieter candidate may still show the behavioral strengths needed for the role.

### Key hiring benefits of behavioral assessments:

- More consistent hiring decisions across managers and teams

- Less reliance on gut feel or unstructured interview feedback

- Better understanding of candidate fit beyond experience and technical skills

- Stronger evidence for interview questions and follow-up conversations

- Clearer insight into potential workplace strengths and risks

- More structured recruitment decisions as hiring volume increases

The practical outcome? Hiring teams can make decisions with more clarity, less guesswork and a better understanding of how a candidate may actually work once they join.

## Types of Behavioral Assessments

There are several types of behavioral assessments, and each gives hiring teams a different kind of insight. Some are based on direct observation. Others use self-report questionnaires, workplace simulations or context-specific evaluation methods.

For recruitment, the best choice depends on the role, the hiring stage and the type of behavioral evidence you need.

Type of behavioral assessmentWhat it involvesStrengthsLimitations

Direct assessmentsObserving behavior in a real or controlled setting.Useful for seeing behavior in action.Can be time-intensive and harder to scale.

Indirect assessmentsGathering insight through questionnaires, self-reports or manager input.Scalable and easy to compare across candidates.Relies on accurate responses and careful interpretation.

Analog assessmentsUsing simulations or role-based exercises.Shows how someone may respond to realistic scenarios.May not capture every part of the actual role.

Idiographic assessmentsLooking at behavior in relation to the individual’s own patterns and context.Highly personalised and nuanced.Less standardised for high-volume recruitment.

Contextual assessmentsEvaluating behavior in relation to a specific environment or situation.Strong for role and culture fit.Requires clear role criteria to be useful.

Most organizations use a combination of methods rather than relying on one behavioral assessment test alone. For example, a hiring team might use an online behavioral questionnaire before interview, then explore the results through structured interview questions or a practical task.

That combination gives a fuller picture: what the candidate says, how they are likely to behave, and how those behaviors relate to the role.

## Direct Behavioral Assessments

Direct behavioral assessments involve observing how someone behaves in a real or controlled situation. In a hiring context, this could include work sample tasks, assessment centre exercises, role plays, group activities or practical simulations that reflect the demands of the job.

The main advantage is that hiring teams can see behavior in action. Not just what a candidate says they would do, but how they actually respond when faced with a relevant task or scenario.

For example, a direct behavioral assessment for a sales role might involve a simulated client conversation. For a leadership role, it might involve a group discussion where the candidate needs to influence others, manage competing views and keep the task moving. For a customer-facing role, it might test how someone handles a difficult conversation under pressure.

## Indirect Behavioral Assessments

Indirect behavioral assessments gather insight through a person’s responses, feedback from others or structured questionnaires. In recruitment, this often means asking candidates to complete a behavioral assessment test online before or during the interview stage.

These assessments typically ask candidates to respond to statements, scenarios or preference-based questions. The results are then used to identify likely workplace behaviors, such as how someone communicates, approaches problems, handles pressure or works with others.

For hiring teams, indirect assessments are useful because they are easier to scale than live observation. Every candidate can complete the same assessment, results can be reviewed consistently, and hiring managers can use the output to guide more focused interview conversations.

For example, a behavioral profile may suggest that a candidate is likely to prefer autonomy, fast decisions and direct communication. That does not mean they are automatically right or wrong for a role. It gives the interviewer a starting point. How has that style helped them in previous roles? Where has it created challenges? What support would help them perform well?

## Other Behavioral Assessment Approaches

Other behavioral assessment approaches include analog, idiographic and contextual assessments. These methods are often used when hiring teams need more role-specific or situation-specific insight.

### Analog assessments

Analog assessments use simulated environments to understand how someone may behave in a similar real-world situation. In recruitment, this could include role plays, case studies, inbox exercises, presentations or scenario-based judgement tasks. They are especially useful when the role involves complex interpersonal decisions, such as handling customer complaints, leading a team through change or prioritising competing demands.

### Idiographic assessments

Idiographic assessments focus on the individual’s own behavioral patterns rather than comparing every candidate against a broad general profile. They look at how someone behaves in relation to their own context, motivations, experiences and triggers. This can be helpful for leadership development or internal mobility, where the organization already has more information about the person and wants a deeper view of how they may grow.

### Contextual assessments

Contextual assessments evaluate behavior in relation to a specific role, team or work environment. This matters because the same behavioral style can be an advantage in one setting and a challenge in another. A candidate who enjoys fast decisions and limited structure may thrive in a scaling sales team. They may find a highly process-led compliance environment more frustrating.

For hiring teams, these approaches are most useful when role requirements are clear. Without that context, assessment results can become too broad to guide a decision. With it, they can help employers understand not just what a candidate is like, but where that candidate is most likely to perform well.

## Behavioral Assessment Examples

Behavioral assessment examples can make the concept easier to understand. In recruitment, these assessments are not about judging whether a candidate has a “good” or “bad” personality. They are about identifying likely workplace behaviors and exploring how those behaviors may show up in the role.

A behavioral assessment might highlight that a candidate is likely to:

- Communicate in a direct, confident way

- Prefer fast-moving environments with clear goals

- Take initiative when solving problems

- Need variety to stay engaged

- Avoid highly repetitive or process-heavy work

- Build relationships quickly with new colleagues or customers

In a leadership context, a behavioral assessment might show that someone is calm under pressure, collaborative and good at creating structure, which could support people management, coaching and team stability. But if the role needs urgent transformation, the hiring team may want to explore how confidently the candidate challenges existing ways of working.

For team fit, behavioral assessments can also reveal how a new hire may work with others. A candidate who prefers independence may thrive in a role with autonomy, but may need clear expectations in a highly collaborative team. Someone who values harmony may bring a team together, but may need support with difficult conversations.

## Behavioral Assessments vs Other Candidate Assessments

Behavioral assessments are one part of a wider candidate assessment strategy. They help hiring teams understand how someone is likely to behave at work, but they do not measure everything a role may require. A candidate might have the behavioral style to succeed in a role but lack the required technical ability. Another might score strongly on aptitude but struggle with the communication style, pace or collaboration demands of the team.

Assessment typeWhat it measuresStrengthsLimitationsBest used for

Behavioral assessmentsWorkplace behaviors, communication style, decision-making preferences and likely work patterns.Helps hiring teams understand how someone may approach the role, team and working environment.Should not be used as the only evidence for hiring decisions.Understanding role fit, team fit, management style and workplace behavior.

A behavioral assessment might help you understand whether a candidate prefers pace, structure, autonomy or collaboration. An aptitude test might show how quickly they can solve new problems. A personality assessment may give broader insight into long-term preferences. An emotional intelligence assessment can help explore how they understand themselves and respond to others.

Used together, these assessments give hiring teams a more balanced view. Not just “Can this person do the job?” but “How are they likely to do the job, and what support will help them succeed?”

## Benefits of Behavioral Assessments for Recruitment

The benefits of behavioral assessments for recruitment are strongest when they help hiring teams make clearer, more consistent and more role-relevant decisions. They are not just a way to “profile” candidates. Used properly, they turn behavioral insight into practical hiring evidence.

### Better hiring decisions

Interviews can be useful, but they are often inconsistent. Different managers may ask different questions, value different behaviors or interpret answers in different ways.

Behavioral assessments give teams a shared language for discussing how a candidate may work, not just what they have done before. That helps hiring managers move beyond first impressions and focus on evidence that relates directly to the role.

### Improved quality of hire

A candidate may look strong on paper and interview well, but still struggle in the role if their working style clashes with the environment.

For example, someone who needs high autonomy may find a tightly controlled role frustrating. Someone who prefers detail and structure may struggle in a role where priorities change daily. Behavioral insight helps hiring teams spot these points earlier.

### Stronger team fit

Better team fit does not mean hiring people who are all the same. Quite the opposite.

Behavioral assessments can help managers understand where a candidate may complement the existing team, where they may create healthy challenge and where they may need support to collaborate well.

### Reduced turnover risk

For recruitment teams dealing with turnover, behavioral assessments can support better expectation-setting before a hiring decision is made.

When managers understand how someone is likely to communicate, respond to pressure and stay motivated, onboarding can be more tailored from day one. That can reduce early friction and help new starters settle into the role with clearer guidance.

### More consistent recruitment at scale

As organizations grow, more hiring decisions are made by more people across more teams. Without structure, hiring standards can drift.

Behavioral assessment recruitment processes help create a more repeatable approach, especially when combined with defined role criteria and structured interviews.

### Key takeaway: benefits of behavioral assessments for recruitment

- They help hiring teams compare candidates using consistent behavioral evidence.

- They reduce over-reliance on gut feel, confidence or interview performance alone.

- They support better role fit by linking behavior to real workplace demands.

- They help managers identify likely strengths, risks and support needs before hiring.

- They can improve onboarding by giving managers clearer insight into how new hires may work best.

- They support scalable recruitment by creating a shared framework across teams.

Most teams do not need assessment data for the sake of it. They need insight they can actually use. That is where behavioral assessments add value: they turn candidate behavior into clearer hiring conversations.

## Limitations and Considerations

Behavioral assessments can improve hiring decisions, but they should not be used as a single source of truth. They are most useful when they sit within a structured recruitment process that also includes interviews, role criteria, skills evidence and candidate context.

### Assessments should not be used alone

A behavioral assessment can show likely workplace preferences and tendencies. It cannot tell you everything about a candidate’s capability, experience, motivation or future performance.

That is why behavioral assessment results should support hiring decisions, not replace them. The strongest approach is to use them alongside structured interviews, aptitude assessments, work samples and role-specific questions.

### Candidate context matters

Behavior does not exist in isolation, and a candidate’s working style may look different depending on the role, manager, team culture and level of support available.

For example, someone who appears cautious may be highly effective in a detail-heavy role. Someone who appears assertive may be valuable in a fast-moving commercial environment, but may need support in a role that requires high diplomacy. The question is not whether a behavior is “good” or “bad”. It is whether it fits the role context.

### Results need careful interpretation

Behavioral assessment tools are only as useful as the way results are interpreted. Hiring managers need to understand what the assessment measures, what it does not measure and how to discuss results fairly with candidates.

This is where training and guidance matter as you implement behavioral assessments into your process. Without it, there is a risk of over-simplifying results or treating a behavioral profile as a fixed label.

### Candidate experience should be protected

Assessments can improve hiring, but only when candidates understand why they are being used. A long or unclear behavioral assessment test can create frustration, especially if candidates receive no feedback or do not understand how the results will be considered.

### Combine assessments with structured interviews

The best use of behavioral assessments is often in interview preparation. Results can help hiring managers ask more targeted questions, explore potential strengths and risks, and create a more evidence-led conversation.

## How Behavioral Assessments Fit Into Modern Hiring Platforms

Behavioral assessments often become more useful when they are built into a wider hiring platform. On their own, assessment results can give hiring managers valuable insight. But when they are connected to role requirements, candidate workflows and interview guidance, they become easier to apply consistently.

### From standalone assessment to hiring workflow

In a modern recruitment process, behavioral assessment tools can sit alongside application screening, structured interviews, aptitude assessments and hiring manager feedback. Behavioral insight can help recruiters shortlist candidates, guide interview questions or support final-stage decision-making.

### Candidate benchmarking

A behavioral assessment platform can help teams compare candidate results against role-specific requirements. This is not about finding a “perfect” personality type. It is about understanding how closely a candidate’s likely working style aligns with the behaviors needed for success.

### Interview guidance

One of the most practical uses of behavioral assessments is interview preparation. Assessment platforms can turn results into suggested questions, discussion prompts or areas to explore. That gives hiring managers a clearer way to use the data. Instead of reading a report and making assumptions, they can ask targeted questions that are much more useful than additional generic competency questions.

### Recruitment analytics and hiring consistency

When behavioral assessments are connected to hiring workflows, organizations can also build a more consistent recruitment process across teams. This can help standardise how assessments are used, how feedback is captured and how decisions are reviewed. Over time, recruitment analytics may also help teams understand where candidates drop out, which roles require stronger assessment criteria, or where hiring managers need extra support.

### Summary: business outcomes of integrated behavioral assessments

- More consistent use of assessment data across hiring teams

- Clearer links between role requirements and candidate evidence

- Better interview preparation for hiring managers

- Stronger candidate benchmarking and comparison

- More structured recruitment workflows at scale

- Improved visibility across hiring decisions and outcomes

The goal is not to make hiring feel automated or impersonal, but to give people better structure, better insight and fewer opportunities for guesswork.

## How to Use Behavioral Assessments in the Hiring Process

Behavioral assessments work best when they are built into a clear hiring process, not added at the end as an afterthought. The aim is to connect assessment insight to the role, the interview and the final decision. Used this way, behavioral assessments in hiring can help teams compare candidates more fairly, ask better questions and make decisions with stronger evidence.

### 1. Define the role requirements

Start by clarifying what success looks like in the role. Not just responsibilities or qualifications, but the behaviors someone will need to perform well.

For example, does the role require:

- Fast decision-making?

- High attention to detail?

- Frequent collaboration?

- Resilience under pressure?

- Strong customer communication?

- Comfort with ambiguity?

- Independent problem-solving?

This step matters because behavioral data is only useful when you know what you are comparing it against. A candidate’s style may be a strength in one role and a challenge in another.

### 2. Select the right assessment type

Choose behavioral assessment tools that match the hiring need. For early-stage screening, a scalable online behavioral assessment test may be useful. For senior or complex roles, you may want to combine behavioral insight with structured interviews, simulations or additional psychometric assessments.

### 3. Assess candidates consistently

Every candidate for the same role should complete the same assessment at the same stage of the process. Consistency also protects hiring teams from drifting back into subjective decision-making. If one candidate is assessed formally and another is judged only through interview impressions, the evidence base becomes uneven.

### 4. Interpret results in context

Assessment results should be reviewed against the role requirements, not in isolation. Look for likely strengths, possible risks and areas to explore further. For example, if a candidate appears highly independent, that may be ideal for a role with autonomy. But if the role involves close team coordination, the interviewer may need to explore how the candidate collaborates, shares updates and responds to feedback.

### 5. Combine results with structured interviews

Behavioral assessments become more powerful when they improve the interview conversation. Use the results to create targeted questions that help hiring managers move from generic interview answers to more specific, evidence-led discussion.

### 6. Make an informed hiring decision

At the final stage, bring the evidence together. Behavioral assessment results should be considered alongside interview feedback, experience, aptitude, skills evidence and role requirements.

A simple decision checklist can help:

- Have we defined the behaviors needed for success?

- Did every candidate complete the same assessment process?

- Have we interpreted the results in relation to the role?

- Did we use the assessment to guide structured interview questions?

- Have we considered both strengths and potential support needs?

- Are we making the decision based on evidence, not instinct alone?

The strongest hiring decisions come from a balanced view of capability, behavior, motivation and fit.

## Choosing the Right Behavioral Assessment Tool

Choosing the right behavioral assessment tool starts with one question: what decision are you trying to improve? For recruitment, the tool should help hiring teams understand role-relevant behavior, compare candidates consistently and use the results in a fair, practical way. A polished report is not enough. The assessment needs to support better hiring conversations.

### Assessment validity

Validity tells you whether an assessment measures what it claims to measure. For hiring, this matters because behavioral insight may influence interview questions, shortlisting decisions or final candidate evaluation. Look for behavioral assessment tools that are backed by clear methodology, psychometric evidence and transparent guidance.

### Reliability

Reliability refers to the consistency of the assessment. If a tool produces wildly different results without good reason, it becomes difficult to trust. A reliable behavioral assessment platform should give hiring teams confidence that results are stable enough to inform structured conversations. Not absolute predictions. Useful signals.

### Reporting quality

The best reports do more than describe a candidate. They help hiring managers act on the insight. Strong behavioral assessment reports should be clear, role-relevant and easy to interpret. They might include likely strengths, potential risks, interview prompts, management guidance or onboarding suggestions.

### Ease of use

If an assessment is difficult to administer, it may not be used consistently. That creates problems for fairness, candidate experience and hiring quality. Look for tools that fit naturally into your recruitment workflow. Recruiters should be able to invite candidates, track completion, access reports and share insights without adding unnecessary admin.

### Candidate experience

A behavioral assessment test should feel relevant, respectful and easy to complete. Candidates should know why they are being asked to take it, how long it will take and how the results will be used. This matters more than many teams realise, as a confusing assessment process can damage trust, especially for strong candidates who are comparing multiple employers.

### Platform integration

For growing organizations, integration can make a major difference. A behavioral assessment platform that connects with wider hiring workflows can help teams standardise assessment use, benchmark candidates and keep evidence in one place. This is particularly useful when recruitment is happening across multiple teams, regions or hiring managers.

### Hiring objectives

Finally, match the tool to your hiring objectives. Are you trying to improve quality of hire? Reduce turnover? Build more consistent interviews? Support graduate recruitment? Identify leadership potential? Different objectives may require different assessment combinations. Behavioral assessments may work best alongside aptitude assessments, personality assessments, emotional intelligence assessments or structured interview frameworks.

## Why Organizations Use Thomas for Behavioral Assessments

Organizations use Thomas for behavioral assessments when they want to understand how people are likely to work, communicate and perform across the employee lifecycle. Thomas behavioral assessments are based on DISC theory, which looks at behavioral preferences linked to dominance, influence, steadiness and compliance.

### Behavioral insight for hiring

For recruitment teams, Thomas behavioral assessments can support more structured candidate conversations. Results can help hiring managers explore how someone is likely to:

- Communicate with colleagues, managers and customers

- Respond to pressure or changing priorities

- Approach targets, detail and deadlines

- Work independently or collaboratively

- Adapt to the expectations of the role

This gives hiring teams a clearer way to discuss behavioral fit without relying only on interview impressions.

### Support beyond recruitment

The same insight can support onboarding, management conversations, team development and employee growth. For example, a manager may use behavioral insight to understand how a new starter prefers to receive feedback, what motivates them, or where they may need extra structure.

### Part of a broader assessment ecosystem

Thomas sits within a wider talent assessment ecosystem, which may include behavioral, aptitude, personality, emotional intelligence and 360-degree feedback assessments. Each gives a different view of candidate or employee potential.

Where behavioral assessments fit within Thomas

- Hiring: Understand candidate behavior and role fit.

- Onboarding: Help managers support new starters more effectively.

- Team development: Improve communication and collaboration.

- Leadership development: Explore behavioral strengths and potential risks.

- Talent management: Support more informed people decisions across the employee lifecycle.

The value for organizations is not just the assessment itself. It is the ability to turn behavioral insight into better conversations, clearer decisions and more consistent people processes.

## FAQs About Behavioral Assessments

### What is a behavioral assessment?

In hiring, behavioral assessments help employers explore work-related preferences such as communication style, decision-making, motivation, adaptability and teamworking. They add another layer of evidence alongside CVs, interviews and skills-based assessments.

### What do behavioral assessments measure?

Behavioral assessments measure workplace behaviors, preferences and tendencies that influence how someone may perform in a role. They often explore areas such as communication style, collaboration and teamworking, decision-making preferences, motivation, adaptability, response to pressure, leadership behaviors, and potential workplace strengths and risks.

### What do behavioral assessments measure?

Behavioral assessments measure workplace behaviors, preferences and tendencies that influence how someone may perform in a role. They often explore areas such as communication style, collaboration and teamworking, decision-making preferences, motivation, adaptability, response to pressure, leadership behaviors, and potential workplace strengths and risks.

### What is the primary goal of behavioral assessment?

The primary goal of behavioral assessment is to make people decisions more structured and evidence-led. For recruitment teams, that means understanding how a candidate may work in practice, not just what they have done before. Behavioral assessments can help hiring managers ask better interview questions, compare candidates more consistently and identify where someone may need support to succeed.

### What is an example of a behavioral assessment?

An example of a behavioral assessment is an online questionnaire that explores how a candidate prefers to communicate, make decisions and respond to pressure. For instance, a candidate may complete a behavioral assessment test before interview. The results might suggest they prefer fast-paced work, direct communication and autonomy. A hiring manager could then use that insight to ask targeted questions about collaboration, attention to detail and how the candidate manages changing priorities.

### When should behavioral assessments be used?

Behavioral assessments should be used when hiring teams need clearer insight into how candidates are likely to work, communicate and fit the role. They can be useful during shortlisting, interview preparation, final-stage decision-making and onboarding. They are especially valuable for roles where communication, collaboration, leadership, resilience or customer interaction are important.

### Are behavioral assessments accurate?

Behavioral assessments can be accurate and useful when they are valid, reliable and interpreted in context. They should not be treated as perfect predictions of future performance; the strongest approach uses behavioral assessments alongside structured interviews, aptitude tests, work samples and other role-relevant evidence.

### How do behavioral assessments compare to aptitude tests?

Behavioral assessments explore how someone is likely to behave at work, while aptitude tests assess ability or potential. An aptitude test may show how quickly a candidate can solve problems, interpret information or learn new skills. A behavioral assessment shows how they may communicate, collaborate, respond to pressure or approach tasks.

### How do behavioral assessments compare to personality assessments?

Behavioral assessments focus on observable workplace behavior, while personality assessments explore broader traits and preferences. There is some overlap, but the use case is different. Behavioral assessments are often more directly linked to how someone may act in a role or team. Personality assessments can give a wider view of underlying tendencies, long-term preferences and development needs.

## Behavioral Assessments and Better Hiring Decisions

Behavioral assessments help hiring teams make better decisions by adding structure, consistency and role-relevant insight to the recruitment process. They help employers understand how candidates are likely to communicate, collaborate, respond to pressure and approach the work they will actually be doing.

The strongest hiring decisions are rarely based on one factor: CVs show experience, interviews reveal motivation, and aptitude tests can highlight capability. Behavioral assessments add another important layer: how someone may behave in the role, with the team and within the working environment.

Used well, behavioral assessments support evidence-based hiring without removing human judgement. They help hiring managers ask better questions, compare candidates more fairly and identify where a new hire may need support to succeed.

#
Ultimate Guide to Leadership Assessments & Tests

9 minutes |

Updated
03 October 2025

By
Duncan Stimpson

We have all come across good and bad leaders in our time, but, how do we know to choose someone who can fulfill the role of a great leader? It’s the debate many businesses have over their lifetime, and for those looking for business success, a great leader in a team can be the difference between hitting targets or staying in the slow lane.

In this guide we are going to take a look at what a leadership assessment is, how they can be used to find the talent, the different types of leadership and how Thomas can help you find the leaders in your organization.

We have a body of tools and resources that are ready to be used to understand more about leaders and practical ways of developing great leaders in every team. .

## What is a leadership assessment?

A leadership assessment test is designed to help employers identify an individual’s ability to lead, manage, and direct others. Do they have what it takes to become a leader in their teams and within the business? That’s what a leadership assessment is designed to answer.

Businesses spend countless hours training staff, trying to perfect systems and create better work environments, but leadership has always been a big debate. Many have found themselves in management positions but have struggled to lead whilst those who want to lead may be getting overlooked for a variety of reasons.

The debate, can leadership be taught or is it inherent rages - but leadership assessments bring social science to the foreground looking at characteristics, behaviors and even temperament to uncover who may be the leader that the business requires, or didn’t even realize they had under their noses.

When recruiting for leaders within an organization one of the key elements is also understanding the business world that we live in. Leadership takes many different forms and different types of leadership styles are required in an ever changing world that we live in, that’s where leadership assessment comes into play. Understanding who has the kinds of characteristics and attitudes to these new styles of working is of great advantage.

Finding staff that have the aptitude and characteristics to lead is the biggest challenge. Whether it is succession planning, workforce development or even lateral hiring within an organisation knowing what to look for is absolutely essential in creating the right environment to build a leader within a team.

## How leadership tests are used in organisations

Leadership tests are used to identify and describe individuals' abilities and skills as they refer to leading, managing and directing others and how their characteristics and skills fit into their leadership positions. Leadership tests are used to take account of the present and future ability of a given person and position.

Leadership tests can be used to identify candidates who are:

- Starting their career in the business and demonstrate the potential or lack of potential to be a leader

- Those looking to improve their career chances and develop their position within the business

- For succession planning, especially in well-established organizations who are looking for someone to carry the culture of the business forward

Using the right kinds of tests is also essential in identifying the leadership characteristics. We will look at what the different styles of leadership look like later on.

Having good leaders is also important for a company’s overall success, productivity and reducing turnover by creating loyalty and improving the general mood of the employees. The opposite can be said for business leaders who are the exact opposite.

A manager who possesses good leadership skills is thus an asset for the company. This is why many organizations are turning to leadership assessments to help them identify leadership candidates with leadership skills.

Finally, leadership roles are directly related to the future success or failure of a business. Using these kinds of tests helps identify who can lead and who can create the future vision of the business.

## What leadership ability tests measure

Leadership ability tests are designed to measure a number of things specific to the characteristics of great leaders. This includes things like, self confidence, emotional intelligence and even providing a compelling vision of the future. We are going to take a look at some of these areas and give a more brief insight into these leadership characteristics. Remember, all of these areas can be tested through questions on leadership assessments.

### Self confidence

How you deal with set-backs and the way you talk to yourself can be measured in these tests. Understanding that self confidence is part of what makes a great leader is key. Knowing that you add real value to your work and to those around you is the starting point.

### Positive attitude, resilience and outlook

Do you see the glass half full or half empty? A positive attitude and outlook is essential to leadership, helping to navigate others during times of uncertainty. This kind of attitude builds confidence and inspires others to see things with a positive mindset in the long run.

### Emotional intelligence (EQ)

Emotional Intelligence or EQ as it otherwise known is the ability to recognize feelings - your own and those of others - and manage those emotions to create strong relationships. Having this soft set of skills is essential in building teams and trust in those teams to develop the business moving forwards.

### Vision and strategic thinking

It’s one thing to lead, it’s another to get others to see what it is you’re trying to create. Think of Steve Jobs and Elon Musk - they have the ability to make others see very clearly where the business is headed. If you can communicate with your team what you want to achieve, you will find more people joining your vision than dispelling it.

### Motivating and inspiring others

Once you have shown that vision and compelled people to chase it, can you motivate them to deliver it? Can you find a way of communicating with what they need to make it a reality? That’s a key part of the leadership development process.

### Managing performance effectively

Can you manage individuals and teams effectively? How are they performing and how can you make them perform better? These are key questions to be able to answer when becoming a leader.

If you can assess a candidate on these elements, you will be able to see who will have a more rounded approach (think hard and soft skills) to those who can inspire a vision for the future (dreamers).

## The different types of leadership styles

There are of course different types of leadership. Each style will have advantages and disadvantages and the industry you operate in will call for different styles of leadership because it suits the industry. We are going to take a closer look at these different types of leadership styles.

### Democratic leadership

This is rooted in democratic theory which involves other members of the team in the decision making process. The leader will normally have the last word in the decision making process but team members feel engaged with the process and motivated to contribute. Disagreements however can take up time and slow down decision making time.

### Autocratic leadership

This is rooted in autocratic theory where the leader makes all the decisions and there is no room for discussion for any alternative theory. Autocratic leaders make decisions based on their own theories and beliefs and have no time for others in the process.

### Laissez faire leadership

This leadership style is completely opposite to the autocratic style. Instead of a single leader making decisions for everyone else, laissez faire leaders make few decisions and let everyone else choose their own workplace solutions.

### Strategic leadership

This is someone who is loyal to the company and the organization’s vision but believes in transparency, effective communication, problem-solving, delegation, passion for their job, compassion, and empathy for others and self-awareness. The aim is to get others to see the company vision and work towards the same goal.

### Transformational leadership

In transformational leadership, the leader is using their skills to show the vision of the company of the future and using different skills that encourages and empowers individuals to go after that same vision.

### Transactional leadership

Transactional leadership is about the ‘give and take’ principles of management where the leader uses things such as rewards and punishments in order to achieve business goals. This is about ensuring that the day to day gets carried out the way that it needs to be over anything else.

### Charismatic leadership

This is a leadership style that is concerned with getting others to carry out their vision or goals through the use of eloquent communication, persuasion and force of personality. This is very common in leaders who have a very ethereal style of communicating, coming across almost as divine.

### Bureaucratic leadership

Just the word bureaucratic should say everything you need to know. This is leadership that is concerned with a formalized set of processes, procedures, and structures. There is a hierarchy of authority and everything is very well laid out to avoid confusion.

Through leadership assessment tools, you can begin to understand what kind of leaders you may have in your organization.

## How Thomas can help you to identify and develop leaders

Using the globally recognized and respected 'Big 5' psychological theory Thomas' Personality assessment (also known as the High Potential Trait Indicator, or HPTI), helps you to understand if someone is well suited to a certain job role or position. Assessing six core traits (Conscientiousness, Adjustment, Curiosity, Risk Approach, Ambiguity Acceptance and Competitiveness) it can also help you to identify leadership potential, adding confidence to your recruitment.

Whether you are looking for the next superstar to join your team, possibly even start to change team dynamics or you want to measure the level of conscientiousness in your workplace, the Thomas assessment platform allows you to recruit with data, not just gut feel.

Johnsons Workwear successfully delivers its workwear services to more than 36,000 clients across a broad range of industry sectors throughout the UK. Headquartered in Fulwood, Preston and employing more than 2,300 staff across 17 sites, Johnsons Workwear sets the bar high in the customer service that it delivers and the continued investment in its people.

## The Challenge

Johnsons Workwear had an ambitious plan for sustained business growth, nurturing a pool of talent was recognised as being a critical factor to success. However, attracting the best talent into the world of industrial laundry was proving to be costly and challenging and the training of new recruits was often a lengthy and complex process. In 2017, the idea to launch the Johnsons Academy, a year-long executive sponsored talent management programme, took shape. With limited spaces available, they needed a way to identify the 12 candidates with the highest potential to join the Academy.

“We needed to get a clear picture of each individual’s talents, personality and behaviours so that we could tailor a development programme to meet their needs. Equally important was the need for candidates to gain a deeper understanding of themselves and their own potential away from their day-to-day jobs.” – Michela Deegan, Learning and Development Manager.

## The Solution

The solution was to combine the feedback from the PPA profiles conducted at the beginning of the programme with the HPTI (High Potential Trait Indicator) for relevant individuals. This gave the Learning & Development team a wealth of information around each candidate’s behavioural and personality traits, potential frustrations and showed how they were likely to behave under pressure. The feedback also gave an insight into each candidate’s strengths, the areas they needed to develop and a deeper insight into where they could be of most value to the Johnsons Workwear business. The report profiles gave Johnsons Workwear the foundation on which to build solid, individual development plans to further the talent management programme.

“The combined use of the Thomas PPA and HPTI tools has been critical to the continued success of the Johnsons Academy. The report profiles have given us the foundation on which to build solid, individual development plans and to further tailor the talent management programme to meet our Academy candidates’ needs. The profiles also provided a huge step forward for candidates to gain a deeper understanding of themselves and their capabilities as well as giving them sight of where they might excel in future within the Johnsons Workwear business” stated Michela. “For our senior team members, who are highly skilled and experienced people, HPTI has helped to bring clarity to conversations on where to go next helping us to put leadership action plans in place.”

## The Results

The Johnsons Academy has proven to be a huge success with over 70% of 2017 Academy graduates receiving a promotion within 18 months of completion.

Peter Egan, CEO, commented “We truly believe our people are our greatest asset. That’s why we’ve created the Johnsons Academy, to encourage the talent

within the business and to help our rising stars to develop. We are delighted with

the results achieved so far and working with the Thomas range of assessment

tools has been instrumental to the success of our programme.” Egan added

“Winning the award is the icing on the cake – the real reward has been retaining

and developing talented people from within our business and witnessing a huge

increase in staff motivation.”

In the 2018 group, over 10% were promoted in a short period of time, including one into a senior management role. Further endorsement of the success of the Johnsons Academy has come from winning the 2018 Personnel Today Award for Talent Management as well as being nominated as a finalist in the 2019 HR Excellence Awards for Best Talent Management Strategy.

## The Challenge

One of the United Kingdom’s leading universities is “absolutely committed to development”, not only of its students, but of its teaching staff, according to their Talent and Organisational Development Consultant, who explains, “For academics, development is about academic promotion, but for professional services personnel it is about career development within their discipline, which might not mean becoming a more senior manager, but becoming an expert in a particular area.”

With many companies freezing recruitment due to the recession, widespread retention challenges and widening skill gaps, development is increasingly important for all organisations. The consultant explains, “Even during the pandemic, we continued with our career and skill development programmes. We have a wider University Strategy and a People and Culture Strategy. As part of the latter, we look at staff wellbeing, progression and development.”

Faced with the pandemic crisis, the university introduced a new development programme, aimed at increasing the self-awareness of academic and professional services staff. The consultant says, “We have existing senior leadership development programmes and programmes for early career managers for both our academic community and professional services staff. However, we had identified a gap between early career management and senior leadership, so we created a new leadership development programme in 2020. We wanted to make it as broad and engaging as possible, so as well as workshop activity, it involves action learning alongside psychometrics.”

## The Solution

At a time when many organisations were halting development activities, the university introduced a new programme to support its people during a universally challenging time. “The objective was to offer delegates on this new modular programme the opportunity to try something new and be able to do so in a confidential setting. We use psychometrics a lot in our leadership development programmes and wanted to differentiate this programme by using a different provider. We liked the fact that Thomas assessments could be used very effectively for development purposes.”

“Completion of the assessments is a core part of the programme, and individuals also have the option of having one-to--one feedback on the longer report. The profiles aren't shared with delegates’ line managers unless they choose to do so. We do not use the assessment to inform any promotional decisions, it is purely for their self-awareness and personal development. However, the line managers do have to endorse their direct reports’ applications to the programme, and we run sessions to offer line managers guidance in how to support participants, and how they might create space for participants to put their learning into practise in their local area.”

“The connections with colleagues from other parts of the institution is important for us. We operate with devolved, local accountabilities, which can make it quite difficult to introduce programmes that are suitable for all, but there are more commonalities than someone might expect in what is quite a complex organisation. We chose to include the Aptitude assessment because it offers delegates the opportunity to find out how they learn and develop in a confidential setting. At a later stage, we will be undertaking 360-degree feedback, and we are keen to incorporate this element of the programme into a much broader offering with respect to career development.”

## The Results

Although the university is yet to see the long-term impacts of the programme, it is actively engaged in monitoring these, with a strong focus on data analytics. Reflecting on the results so far, the university consultant says, “So far, we have seen encouraging signs, such as the fact that the programme itself is oversubscribed. Word travels, and we see more people taking up the programme after hearing about the experiences of early adopters.”

“I've been giving participants feedback on the assessments, and it's been great. We have had about five cohorts of delegates and around 30 to 40% take up the option of having one to one feedback on the longer report. During these sessions, we talk through the alignment or apparent contradictions between the different reports – for instance between their Behaviour and Personality profiles. From an administrative point of view, downloading the reports has been very intuitive. The way that the reports are structured lends itself to feeding back in a fluid way.”

“Academics and professional services staff are engaging with the feedback sessions in approximately the same ratios and they are finding it really useful. The feedback has been extremely positive, and delegates appreciate the opportunity to receive confidential feedback and psychometric insights. Whether the assessments highlighted their ability to manage change or their communication with others, they can then apply learnings to their role and operate differently.”

Ultimately, integrating psychometrics into their leadership development programme is helping to differentiate the university as an employer of choice. “We are finding Assess to be a really great set of assessments for this new leadership programme. Other universities make similar commitments to development, but we do have people joining us from other institutions within the sector, who are surprised by how much we offer.”
